Part One
Introduction

Introduction

Dua is the best act of worship. It is a means of drawing near Allah ‘Azza wa Jall.

This lesson is taken from Qaribun Mujib, a series of Ramadan lessons on du’a. It opens with the du’a: “Rabbi ishrah li sadri wa yassir li amri, wahlul uqdatan min lisani yafqahu qawli. Allahumma ahdi qalbi wa saddid lisani, waslul saqimata qalbi” — a request that Allah open the chest, ease the affair, loosen the knot of the tongue so that the speech may be understood, guide the heart, and set the tongue right.

When a person calls upon Allah, they get to express their pain, their worries, and their concerns before Him. Making du’a is a way of demonstrating dependency on Allah, and of manifesting one’s weakness and neediness before Him. As we continue to call upon Allah, this helps us maintain a constant connection with our Lord, and it helps us continue to have faith in Him.

Chapter One

Why We Call Upon Allah

Dua is the best act of worship. It is a means of drawing near Allah ‘Azza wa Jall. When a person calls upon Allah, they get to express their pain, their worries, their concerns before Him. When a person makes du’a, they are demonstrating their dependency on Allah. They are manifesting their weakness, their neediness before Him.

The fact is that Allah is the one who is perfectly great, and we, His slaves, are the ones who are poor. We are the ones who are in need of Him. We are the ones who are weak. There is no stage of our lives when we can be independent of calling upon Allah. Rather, no matter what stage of our lives we are in, no matter what we are doing, no matter what is happening in our lives, we are in need of calling upon Allah.

As we continue to call upon Allah, this helps us maintain a constant connection with our Lord. And when we call upon Him, this helps us to continue to have faith in Allah, to continue to believe in Him. When we call upon Allah, we are recognizing our neediness, and we are recognizing the fact that we have a Lord who helps, a Lord who cares, a Lord who listens, and a Lord who is able to grant us what we need.

Allah, our Lord, is near. He is Qareeb. He is Mujeeb. He responds to us.

Chapter Two

Al-Qareeb — The Ever-Near

The Qur’an

“And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me by obedience and believe in Me, that they may be rightly guided.”

Allah shows His mercy towards people in this ayah by calling them ‘Ibadi’ — My slaves. And when Allah describes Himself as Qareeb, the one who is near, He is encouraging us to call upon Him. We belong to Allah, and He, the Exalted, is near. He is not far. So we can call upon Him whenever we want, whenever we need.

Hadith — narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash’ari (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu)

We were in the company of the Messenger of Allah salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, travelling, and whenever we went up a high place we would say “La ilaha illallah, Allahu Akbar,” and our voices used to rise. So the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said to us: “O people, be merciful to yourselves — you are not calling upon someone who is deaf or absent. Rather, you are calling upon the One who is with you. He is Sami’un, Qareeb — All-Hearing, Ever-Near.”

So we can call upon Allah in our hearts, or we can whisper to Him, or we can talk to Him in a way that is audible. Allah tells us in Surat Taha: “And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is even more hidden.” There are times we express our du’a verbally, and times we just keep what is in our heart in our heart — we don’t even know what words to use. Allah knows. He hears the call of our heart.

In a narration, a man asked the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam whether their Lord was near, so that they should whisper to Him, or far, so that they should call out to Him audibly. It was in answer to this that the ayah “I am near” was revealed. So call upon Allah however you want — audibly, in a whisper, or in your heart.

Hadith

A Bedouin came to the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam and said, “O Messenger of Allah, teach me something good.” The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam took his hand and taught him to count on his fingers: SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, La ilaha illallah, Allahu Akbar. The man later returned and asked, “All of these words are for Allah — what is there for me?” So the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam told him: when you say Allahu Akbar, Allah says, “Sadaqta” — you have spoken the truth. When you say Alhamdulillah, Allah says the same. When you say “Allahumma-ghfirli” (O Allah, forgive me), Allah says, “I have done that.” When you say “Allahumma-rhamni” (O Allah, have mercy on me), Allah says, “I have done that.” When you say “Allahumma-rzuqni” (O Allah, provide for me), Allah says, “I have done that.”

At times we hesitate asking people for help, or sharing our feelings with them, because people sometimes seem so distant. They are so preoccupied with their own worlds that, even sitting right next to us, they are disconnected. Sometimes a person hears what we are saying but shows no empathy. Over time, we learn to keep everything inside — we learn not to share, not to express our feelings. Allah is not like that. He is near. He is accessible at any time of day or night, in any place. As we learn in a hadith, Allah says: “I am with My slave when he calls upon Me.”

Being Qareeb means qareebun min sama’i du’a — near with respect to listening to our prayers — and qareebun bil-ijabah — near in terms of responding to our prayer.

Illustration used in the lesson

You are such a tiny creature somewhere on this massive Earth, which is somewhere in this massive universe — like a grain of sand on a beach. What are you compared to the entire creation? Yet when you call upon Allah, He hears you. He gives you attention. Do you recognize your worth before Rabbul ‘Alameen, the Lord of the worlds?

And being Qareeb means there is no need of an intermediary between you and your Lord. In this ayah, Allah says, “When My slaves ask you about Me, then indeed I am near” — it does not say “tell them that I am near.” The word “say” is not even there, because Allah is responding directly to His slaves. He does not ask His Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam to relay it. So you are worthy of calling upon Allah directly, because He hears you.

Chapter Three

Al-Mujeeb — The Ever-Responsive

Allah says, “I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me.” This means Allah does not waste the du’a of His slave. He is not preoccupied with something that would distract Him from responding. The question is: who is this caller? It is the one who truly, correctly calls upon Allah — with attentiveness, with hope, with conviction, while removing any barriers that prevent the du’a from being accepted.

Allah says “Ujibu” — I respond. Responding does not necessarily mean a person is given exactly what they asked for. Allah knows how to respond to His slave, what to give, because sometimes we don’t even know ourselves what is good for us, or when is the right time for us to have something. But He responds every time, and He responds in different ways.

We should call upon Allah like Zakariyya (‘alayhis salam), who said: “Never have I been unhappy in my supplication to You, my Lord” — meaning, every time he called upon Allah, he was happy afterward; he was never disappointed, he never failed. The one who calls upon Allah certainly receives something. They are not returned empty-handed.

Allah says: “So they should respond to Me, and they should believe in Me, so that they are rightly guided.” Just as we want Allah to respond to us, we too should respond to Allah when He calls us — when we are called to salah, when Allah addresses us in the Qur’an and gives a command, we should listen and obey, and we should believe in His generosity, His mercy, His judgment, and His decree.

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that the supplication of the servant is accepted as long as he does not supplicate for what includes sin or the cutting of family ties, and as long as he does not become hasty. He was asked what it means to become hasty, and he salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said it is when a person says, “I supplicated and supplicated, and I did not see it being accepted,” and so he loses interest and abandons du’a. We were told not to be hasty — we should keep calling upon Allah, because He is Qareeb and He is Mujeeb.

Chapter Four

Qareebun Mujeeb — The Da’wah of Salih

Surat Hud, ayah 61
The Qur’an — Surat Hud, 11:61

“And to Thamud We sent their brother Salih. He said: O my people, worship Allah, you have no deity other than Him. He has produced you from the earth and settled you in it. So ask forgiveness of Him and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.”

Salih (‘alayhis salam) invited his people to worship Allah alone, reminded them that Allah created them and settled them on the earth, invited them to seek forgiveness and to repent — and then he gave them hope: your Lord is near, He is responsive, so call upon Him.

Illustration used in the lesson

If someone were to offer us, “I am here, I’m listening to you, ask me for anything — I’ve got my checkbook with me, ask me for anything, I will give it to you,” then no matter what we were doing, we would leave it and come and benefit from that opportunity, because we don’t know when else we will have an opportunity like that. Allah is Qareeb, He is ever near; He is Mujeeb, He is ever responsive to His slaves.

Salih taught his people a sequence before calling upon Allah: first, iman — faith in the oneness of Allah; second, shukr — recognition and gratitude for Allah’s favors (and shukr also brings hope, because if Allah has given so much without even being asked, there is hope He will give what is being asked for); third, istighfar — seeking forgiveness for our shortcomings; and fourth, tawbah — repentance, leaving sin with a firm intention to change. Only then does he say, “Inna Rabbi Qareebun Mujeeb” — call upon your Lord.

The opposite of Qareeb is Ba’eed — distant. And someone distant is not necessarily distant in a physical sense. Someone could be sitting right next to you, or living with you in your home, and still be distant, because you have no connection with them — they don’t show empathy, they don’t help, it doesn’t seem like they love you, and when they show harshness, you feel even more distant. Allah ‘Azza wa Jall is Qareeb — He is Ra’uf, He is Rahim. He is kind, He is merciful. He protects us, He provides for us, He guides us.

Chapter Five

What Du’a Actually Means

Linguistically, the word du’a is from da’a – yad’u, from the masdar du’a or da’wah, and it means to call someone in an audible way, in order to draw their attention to what you are asking for. When it is said “da’awtu Allah” — I made du’a to Allah — it means I prayed to Allah, I asked Him with humility, hoping He will grant me from the good that He has.

Eight Uses of the Word in the Qur’an

  • To summon, as in Surat Ali ‘Imran, ayah 61 — “come, we should call our children and your children”
  • To ask someone to come and help, as in Surat Fatir, ayah 18 — a person heavily laden with sin calling another to bear their burden
  • To proclaim or state a claim, as in Surat al-A’raf, ayah 5
  • To worship, as in Surat al-Kahf — “we will never call upon someone other than Allah as a god”
  • To call to one’s aid, as in Surat al-Baqarah — “call your witnesses”
  • To invite, as Nuh said — “I called my people by night and by day”
  • To assert or name, as in calling someone by the name of their actual father
  • To ask or pray for something — “call upon your Lord”

When we speak of calling upon Allah, du’a means asking Him with humility for the good that He has, and asking Him with hope — expressing extreme humility, neediness, and weakness before Allah; asking Him for what benefits us, and asking for protection from what is harmful.

Two Kinds of Du’a

Du’a al-‘Ibadah is synonymous with worship — a person worships Allah with hope of reward and hope of protection from punishment. Salah, fasting, reciting Qur’an, giving sadaqa, making dhikr — these are all acts of worship, and in doing them, we are hoping for reward and for protection from punishment.

Du’a al-Mas’alah is a request — a person directly asks Allah for something good in this world or the next, and asks Allah to protect them from what is harmful in this world or the next.

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: “Ad-du’au huwal-‘ibadah” — du’a is worship — and he recited: “Your Lord says, call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed those who disdain My worship will enter Hell, rendered contemptible.”

This is similar to how the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said “Al-Hajju ‘Arafah” — Hajj is ‘Arafah. This doesn’t mean Hajj does not include going to Mina, or Muzdalifah, or the ramy, tawaf, or sa’i — all of these rituals are part of Hajj — but the most significant part is ‘Arafah. The one who finds ‘Arafah finds Hajj, and the one who misses ‘Arafah misses Hajj. Likewise, du’a is the essence, the goal, of worship — sometimes we ask Allah verbally, through our words, and sometimes we are calling upon Allah through our state, through our actions — when we pray or recite Qur’an, we are hoping for reward, even without asking verbally.

Chapter Six

The Poverty of Every Creation

The Qur’an — Surat Fatir, 35:15

“O mankind, all of you are in need of Allah, while it is Allah who is Al-Ghani — free of need — and Al-Hamid — praiseworthy.”

What is that phase of our life, or that age, or that time of day or night, when we can say we have no needs? We always have some need or another — we have the need to eat, to breathe, the need for connection, the need to feel loved, the need to feel accepted, the need for security. All of us are fuqara, we are poor, we are in need — and we are in need of Allah, who is the one who is completely independent and owns all treasures.

Everything Belongs to Allah

  • “To Allah belong the treasures of the skies and the earth.” — Surat al-Munafiqun, 63:7
  • “And there is nothing except that with Us are its treasures.” — Surat al-Hijr
  • “And if Allah touches you with something of harm, then there is no remover of it except Him.” — Surat al-An’am, 6:17
Hadith — a man from the tribe of Bul Hujaim asked the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam what his message was

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam replied: “I invite people to Allah alone. He who, when some calamity strikes you, you call upon Him and He removes it from you. And when you are in the wilderness and you lose your way and you call upon Him, He saves you, He guides you. And when you are struck by famine and you call upon Him, He causes plants to grow.”

None of this is in our control. If we have a fever and want to get rid of it, we can have medication upon medication, but it is not going to go away unless Allah allows it. Allah is the one who removes calamity and difficulty, and if He does not guide us back when we are lost, we will be lost forever. Everything in the heavens and the earth depends upon Allah — as we learn in Surat al-Rahman, whoever is in the skies and whoever is in the earth calls upon Allah, and every day He is bringing about something new.

Chapter Seven

Four Kinds of People

One of the scholars said that people fall into four categories with respect to calling upon Allah:

  1. People who neither worship Allah nor ask Him for help — committing a great injustice, since Allah is the one who created them and gave them everything they have.
  2. People who ask Allah for help, and He helps them, but they do not worship Him — even those who do not believe in Allah are helped by Him when they call upon Him in a state of desperation (idtirar).
  3. People who worship Allah and obey Him, but do not ask Him for anything — many Muslims are like this: they do what Muslims are supposed to do, but when they are in difficulty they don’t raise their hands, they don’t humble themselves before Allah.
  4. People who worship Allah and ask Him — He helps them worship and obey Him, and He also helps them in the other matters they ask His help for.
The Qur’an — Surat al-Fatihah

“It is You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

We want to be of the fourth category — the people who worship Allah, and the people who call upon Allah.

Chapter Eight

Why Du’a Is Worth Everything

Allah Himself invites us to call upon Him. In a hadith, we learn that in the last third of the night, Allah addresses people and says: “Is there anyone who will call upon Me, so that I will answer him? Is there anyone who will ask Me for something, so that I give it to him? Is there anyone who seeks forgiveness from Me, so that I forgive him?”

Ask Him for His Favor

Allah tells us to ask Him “of His fadl” — His favor, His surplus, something extra that a person is not necessarily deserving of.

Illustration used in the lesson

If you have employed someone, you pay them what they deserve. But fadl is that you give them more than what you are supposed to pay them. So Allah is telling us to ask Him for things we think we are not deserving of, things we think are extra — ask Him anyway, because Allah is able to give it, and He is very generous.

Allah loves that we ask Him. People do not like being asked for a favor twice or three times — they get tired of it. Allah invites us to call upon Him every night, every day, all the time.

Hadith Qudsi

“O My slaves, all of you are lost except for the one whom I have guided — so seek guidance from Me, and I will guide you. All My slaves, all of you are hungry except those whom I feed — so ask Me for food, I will feed you. All My slaves, all of you are naked except those whom I clothe — so ask Me for clothes, I will clothe you. All My slaves, you commit sin by night and day, and I forgive all sins — so seek forgiveness from Me, I will forgive you. O My slaves, if the first of you and the last of you, and all mankind and all the jinn, were to stand in one open field and ask Me for many things, and I gave every one of them what they asked for, it would not reduce Me in My treasures any more than a needle reduces the ocean when it is dipped into it.”

Hadith — to Ibn ‘Abbas (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhuma)

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: “Ihfazillaha yahfazka” — be mindful of Allah, He will protect you. “Ihfazillaha tajidhu tujahak” — be mindful of Allah, you will find Him before you. “Wa idha sa’alta, fas’alillah” — when you ask, ask Allah. “Wa idhasta’anta, fasta’in billah” — and when you seek help, seek it from Allah.

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: “Laisa shai’un akram ‘alallahi minad-dua” — there is nothing more honorable before Allah than du’a. When you ask people for something, your status decreases in their eyes with every request. When you ask Allah, you become more honorable, because you find Him closer and closer.

Allah Answers the Desperate

The Qur’an — Surat an-Naml, 27:62

“Or who is it who responds to the desperate one (al-mudtarr) when he calls upon Him, and removes the harm?”

Ibn ‘Abbas said this refers to a person in such need that if it is not fulfilled, they will be in great hardship. Other scholars said it refers to someone suffering from extreme poverty, or someone who finds himself disconnected from everyone and everything — completely abandoned, not knowing who to even call, and even if he were trying, maybe his phone is not working, maybe his phone is dead.

But you always have a way of reaching out to Allah. All you have to say is “Ya Allah.” All you have to do is call upon Him, and He is Qareeb, He responds, and He will bring you out of your difficulty.

Hadith

Once people were in great difficulty, and the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said to them: “You have complained of drought in your land. Allah has commanded you to supplicate to Him, and He has promised that He will answer you.”

The King Who Invites Us to Ask

Allah is Malik al-Mulk, the King, the owner of everything — all resources, all treasures, all power are in His hand. Yet He orders us to ask Him. Think about the kings of this world: people who have wealth hide it from others, out of fear that if others see it, they will ask for it.

Illustration used in the lesson

Maybe you have hidden your chocolates or your sweets, or some money that you have, because you are afraid that if your siblings see it, if your children see it, or even if your spouse sees it, they will ask you for it — they will expect you to give them something from it. This is the nature of people, that we are stingy, because we have very limited resources, we are poor. Allah is not poor. He is the King who owns everything, and He invites us to call upon Him.

Difficulty as a Mercy

Ibn al-Qayyim said that when Allah intends good for His slave, He gives the slave the opportunity to be humble and weak before Allah, to be needy before Him. Allah decrees something for the slave because of which the slave is in great need — everything is fine, and then suddenly there is great difficulty that cannot be solved alone. Ibn Taymiyyah said that when Allah intends good for His slave, He inspires him in his heart to call upon Allah, and when the slave calls upon Allah, Allah makes that du’a a means of attaining the good he prayed for. If we had not been in difficulty, we would not have received that good.

Du’a Is a Means of Great Benefit

Hadith

“Supplication benefits against that which has already come and that which has not yet come, so hold fast, O worshippers of Allah, to du’a.”

Imam Ghazali said that du’a repels trials and tribulations, just as a shield is a means of repelling arrows, and just as water is a means of growing plants — when you make du’a, you attain Allah’s mercy, and tribulation is repelled from you.

Hadith

“Indeed Allah is merciful and generous, and He is shy that His slave should raise his hands before Him and He not place something good in them.” And when a Muslim fixes his face before Allah ‘Azza wa Jall — sitting and making du’a for long, consistently, completely focused on Allah — then Allah will definitely give him something, sooner or later.

When it comes to reward for belief and righteous deeds, there is a condition attached. When it comes to du’a, Allah says, “Ud’uni, call upon Me, astajib lakum, I will answer you” — the only condition is that you actually call upon Allah. Even when Iblis asked Allah to grant him a delay until the Day of Judgment, Allah granted it. Iblis lies to us when he whispers that our du’a will not be accepted — don’t believe his lie. Believe what Allah is telling you: “Ujeebu, I respond.”

Nothing turns back the decree except supplication, and nothing increases the lifespan except righteousness. The prophets and the righteous called upon Allah for big things. Look at the du’a of Ibrahim (‘alayhis salam): “Rabbana wab’ath fihim rasulam-minhum yatlu ‘alayhim ayatika” — O Allah, in my offspring, send a messenger. Allah responded to that du’a. Du’a is effective against all trials and difficulties. It is the weapon of the believer, jami’ul khair — something that brings a whole lot of good to a slave.

“Man lam yas’al Allaha yaghdab ‘alayh” — the one who does not ask Allah, then Allah is angry with him. This means the one who asks Allah, Allah is pleased with him. When a person continues to call upon Allah, they learn to become free of dependence on the creation, and they learn to depend on the Creator — they receive closeness to Allah. Without du’a, there is disconnect.

May Allah grant us the joy of calling upon Him, the ability to call upon Him for every little and big thing, and the ability to remember Him and call upon Him the moment we are struck by any challenge — that our first thought is that our Lord is there, He will take care of us, He will answer us, He will help us.

Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdik, ashhadu an la ilaha illa anta, astaghfiruka wa atubu ilaik.
Wassalamu ‘alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
Chapter Nine

He Answers You in Your Salah

Allah ‘Azza wa Jall — our Lord, the Lord of the worlds, our Creator — hears us and responds to us. When we call upon Him, He answers.

Hadith

When a person prays salah and recites Surat al-Fatihah: when the slave says “Alhamdu lillahi Rabbil ‘Alameen,” Allah responds and says, “Hamidani ‘abdi” — My slave has praised Me. When he says “Ar-Rahman Ar-Raheem,” Allah says, “Athna ‘alayya ‘abdi” — My slave has praised Me. When he says “Maliki Yawm id-Din,” Allah says, “Majjadani ‘abdi” — My slave has glorified Me. When he says “Iyyaka na’budu wa iyyaka nasta’in,” Allah says, “Hadha bayni wa bayna ‘abdi, wa li ‘abdi ma sa’al” — this is between Me and My slave, and My slave will have what he asked for. And when he says “Ihdina sirat al-mustaqim...” Allah says, “Hadha li ‘abdi, wa li ‘abdi ma sa’al” — this is for My slave, and My slave will have what he asked for.

Chapter Ten

What Du’a Is, and What It Rests On

Du’a is that a person calls upon his Lord — for relief, for guidance, for aid, for the fulfillment of any need or wish. And this call is not just a call for help; it is an act of worship. It is a great act of worship, very honorable in the sight of Allah, something that Allah loves. It is so important before Him that if a slave abandons du’a, Allah is displeased with that person.

The foundation of this act of worship is tawhid — belief in the oneness of Allah, belief in His absolute perfection, His power, His mercy, His knowledge. Du’a draws a person near to Allah and brings sincerity into the heart. The more a person begins to know Allah and draw near Him, the more he begins to call upon Him — asking Allah for every little and big thing — and the more he learns how to depend on Allah and to trust Allah’s decisions.

Du’a detaches the slave from depending on the creation, and makes the slave depend on Allah alone. When you make du’a, you place your hope in Allah, and you know that Allah is able to do all things — He can say “Kun fa yakun,” be, and it is. So you feel confident, you feel hopeful, you place your trust in Allah.

The Qur’an — Surat al-Baqarah, 2:256

“Whoever disbelieves in taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, one which will never break. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”

As a person increases in their hope and their faith in Allah, their worship becomes stronger, their relationship with Allah becomes stronger, and they begin to find joy and comfort in worshipping Him.

Chapter Eleven

The Real Fruit of Du’a

This is so amazing: a person begins du’a in order to ask Allah for something, but eventually that leads to such a strong connection with Allah that the slave finds closeness to Allah more pleasing than the thing he was praying for.

The real fruit of du’a is not the thing you were asking Allah for. The real fruit of du’a is that you find closeness to Allah — you find joy in talking to Allah, in showing humility before Him, in spending time remembering Him, glorifying Him, praising Him, doing things to earn His approval. That is the real fruit of du’a. You find Allah Qareeb.

Through du’a, our troubles are taken away, our needs are fulfilled, and we receive numerous blessings. But typically, what happens? People only call upon Allah when they are in some difficulty.

The Qur’an — Surat al-Isra, 17:67

When some harm reaches you at sea — when you are travelling through water and a storm hits, or you feel some danger — you forget everyone except Allah. The only one you call upon is Allah. But when He delivers you to land and rescues you, you turn away. And the human being is very ungrateful.

So we should continue to call upon Allah at all times — in difficulty and in ease. The person who attains the real fruit of du’a will continue to call upon Allah even when things are easy, and even after they have received what they prayed for. They will not forget Allah, because they found closeness to Allah by making du’a to Him, and that brought them so much joy that they continue to call upon Him even when they have no problem and are experiencing no difficulty. They will still call Allah. They will still talk to Allah.

Chapter Twelve

No Restriction on Calling Him

There is no fixed time for du’a — it is not that you can only make du’a at a certain time of day or night. You can call upon Allah at any time. Nor is there a certain action required. When it comes to salah, you have to stand in one place, face the qiblah, make wudu, and perform certain actions. Du’a is something you can do while sitting, standing, or lying down; when you have wudu or when you don’t; when you are in your bedclothes, or dressed up for a wedding, or in your work clothes working in the kitchen.

No matter what state you are in, no matter what your condition is, no matter how you are feeling, no matter how busy or free you are — it doesn’t matter. You can call upon Allah at any time, in any state.

And there is no restriction with regard to language. You can call upon Allah in any language. And if you find it difficult to say words of du’a, you can write it, because some people feel they are better able to express themselves when they write. You can know for sure that du’a reaches Allah, because Allah says: “Wa idha sa’alaka ‘ibadi ‘anni fa inni qareeb” — I am near. And the one who is near hears you. The one who is near cares about you. The one who is near is paying attention to you.

The Qur’an — Surat Fatir, 35:10

“Ilayhi yas’adul kalimut tayyib” — good words ascend to Him. And of the good words are the words of du’a. So when you say words of du’a, those words rise up to Allah, and He hears them.

Through du’a, the gates of Jannah are opened up for the slave, and through du’a a person is protected from painful punishment.

Chapter Thirteen

Three Forms of Du’a

1. Praising and Declaring His Oneness

The slave praises and glorifies Allah and declares His oneness. You raise your hands and say, “Ya Allah, la ilaha illa ant” — there is no god but You. You say, “Rabbana lakal hamd” — our Lord, for You is all praise. You are not asking for anything, but this is also du’a.

On the day of ‘Arafah, the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said the best du’a is: “La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul mulku walahul hamd, wa huwa ‘ala kulli shay’in qadir.” In it you are declaring the oneness of Allah and praising Him.

Ayyub (‘alayhis salam), when he was experiencing illness for such a long time, said: “Anni massaniyal durru wa anta arhamur rahimeen” — harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy. He did not ask for anything; he just declared the perfection of Allah. In Surat Ali ‘Imran we find: “Rabbana innaka jami’un nasi li yawmin la rayba feeh” — our Lord, You will gather people on a day about which there is no doubt. And in distress, one of the best things we can say is: “Allahu Allahu Rabbi, la ushriku bihi shay’a” — Allah, Allah is my Lord, I associate no partner with Him.

2. Seeking Forgiveness and Mercy

The slave seeks forgiveness from Allah and asks Allah for His mercy — for example, saying “Allahumma-ghfirli” — O Allah, forgive me.

3. Asking for Something

The slave asks for something — something of dunya, something of akhirah, something in deen, something big, something small, whatever it may be. For example, “Allahumma-rzuqna” — O Allah, provide us sustenance.

Chapter Fourteen

The Way of the Prophets

Adam, Nuh, Yunus, and Ayyub (‘alayhimus salam)

The prophets of Allah are the best example for us, and Allah mentions their stories in the Qur’an to teach us many lessons — among them, how to call upon Him. Within those stories is a description of how they called upon Allah: the words of du’a they used, the kinds of things they prayed for. They are preserved in the Qur’an because Allah is teaching us that this is how you should call upon Him.

Hadith

“Kana idha faza’a faza’a ila salah” — the way of the prophets was that whenever some worry or trouble reached them, they would immediately turn towards salah, towards Allah: O Allah, You help us.

This is a habit we need to develop: the moment something happens, the moment we feel anxious or worried or afraid, stressed out, sensing panic, sad, or overwhelmed — immediately turn towards Allah and ask Him for help. And if you don’t even know what to ask for — for instance when you hear that someone you love has passed away, or that there has been a major accident — we learn in the Qur’an that we should say “Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un” — indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we shall return. This too is a form of du’a: we are not asking for anything specific, rather declaring the perfection of Allah, that we belong to Him and return to Him.

Adam (‘alayhis salam)

When Adam made a mistake, “fatalaqqa Adamu min Rabbihi kalimat” — Adam received from his Lord some words. He learned how to call upon Allah, how to seek forgiveness, how to repent. He and Hawwa said: “Rabbana zalamna anfusana, wa il lam taghfir lana wa tarhamna, lanakunanna minal khasireen” — our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.

At times we feel the same way — that we have really messed up, made a huge mistake. Sometimes the realization comes soon after; sometimes after months, weeks, or years. The moment you realize you have done something wrong, turn to Allah. Don’t just sit with that guilt. Don’t let that guilt eat you up from inside.

What happened when Adam called upon Allah? Allah accepted his repentance. Adam was clearly warned that Shaytan was an enemy to him, clearly told not to eat from the tree — but he was human, and he forgot, and Shaytan tricked him, and he slipped. Then he turned to Allah, and Allah forgave him. When it comes to people, if they give us a clear warning and we still mess up, a lot of times we see no forgiveness and no mercy. Allah is not like that. He accepts repentance over and over again, even for sins which are huge.

Nuh (‘alayhis salam)

Nuh had been calling his people for 950 years. They not only rejected him — they ridiculed him, called him majnun, crazy, and treated him very harshly: “wa qalu majnunun wa dujir.” What did he do in that state? He called upon his Lord: “Anni maghlubun fantasir” — I am defeated, so You help.

Sometimes we get bullied by people we should feel safe with — our own friends, sometimes our own family members. They put us down, they call us crazy, they are harsh with us, they drive us away. Sometimes you feel defeated before your children, before people who are not listening to you or cooperating with you, people making your life very difficult, and you don’t know how to convince them or make them understand. So call upon your Lord, as Nuh did.

And Allah tells us: “Wa laqad nadana Nuhun fa lani’mal mujibun” — Nuh called upon Us, and how excellent are We as those who respond. Allah responded to his du’a, and saved him and his family from the great distress. When you are feeling isolated, when people are ridiculing you and bullying you, and it has been going on for a very long time, this is very distressful — you feel suffocated. Allah saved him from that.

Yunus (‘alayhis salam)

Yunus made a mistake: he became impatient with his people and left them before he was told to, and he was angry with them. He thought Allah would never create constriction for him — he didn’t think he was doing anything wrong. But then he boarded the ship, was thrown into the water, was swallowed by the fish, and found himself in the darkness. What did he say? “La ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu minaz-zalimeen” — there is no god but You, You are perfect, indeed I am of those who do wrong. And Allah tells us: We responded to him and saved him from distress, and that is how We save the believers.

Sometimes it happens that you become hasty in responding to people, in dealing with people. You become impatient, and then you say things and do things that are very damaging. And then there is regret — and in that regret you feel like you are in darkness, that people are angry with you, and you worry that maybe Allah is also displeased with you, and you feel so sad, so worried, so guilty. Even in that condition, call upon Him.

Ayyub (‘alayhis salam)

Ayyub experienced illness, according to some narrations, for eighteen years. If you suffer from any illness for eighteen hours, that is hard. Eighteen days is hard. Eighteen months is hard. Eighteen years is like a lifetime. And he did not only experience illness in his body — he also experienced loss of wealth and loss of his children and family.

His du’a was: “Anni massaniyad-durru wa anta arhamur-rahimeen.” And Allah says: “Fastajabna lahu” — so We responded to him — “fakashafna ma bihi min durrin” — and We removed whatever harm was with him, whatever he was suffering in his body, his family, his wealth — “wa ataynahu ahlahu wa mithlahum ma’ahum” — and We gave him his family, and along with them more. His children increased, and his wealth also doubled. All of this was mercy from Us, and a reminder for the worshippers.

Sometimes when we are in difficulty, the first day we make du’a and things don’t get better; the next day, the next week, and the difficulty just goes on and on. Sometimes it feels like it is getting worse instead of better, and Shaytan says, “See, your du’a is not being answered.” Don’t ever think like that. To say that Allah does not answer is a false statement — it contradicts the statement of Allah, because Allah says, “I respond.” Allah described Ayyub as patient, an excellent worshipper — meaning he did not make du’a just once at the end of eighteen years. He continued to call upon Allah.

Chapter Fifteen

The Way of the Prophets, Continued

Ibrahim, Ya’qub, Yusuf, Musa, Zakariyya, and the Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam

Ibrahim (‘alayhis salam)

Allah describes Ibrahim as “awwahun haleem” — awwah being someone very soft-hearted, who sighs a lot, meaning someone who continues to call upon Allah and continues to humble himself before Him. This shows that Ibrahim experienced great difficulty in his life, and in every difficulty he called upon Allah.

Look at how his own father and his own people treated him: they threw him into the fire. What did he say at that time? “Hasbunallahu wa ni’mal wakeel” — sufficient for us is Allah, and what an excellent trustee He is. And what happened? Yes, he landed in the fire, but Allah turned it into coolness and safety for him. It did not burn him, it did not cause him any pain; rather it became a means of safety.

His father said, “Leave, or I will stone you to death.” So Ibrahim said, “Inni dhahibun ila Rabbi sayahdeen” — I am going to my Lord, my Lord will guide me. And he made du’a: “Rabbi hab li minas-saliheen” — O my Lord, grant me righteous children. “Fa bashsharnahu bi ghulamin haleem” — so We gave him good news of a forbearing boy.

Forbearance is an excellent quality in children: that they are not impulsive, they don’t respond harshly, they don’t get angry and annoyed, they don’t disobey their parents, they are kind and they listen. Sometimes parents yell at their children in a way that is not really fair and can come across as very harsh — but some children are so patient with their parents that they listen to everything and say, “Okay.” They don’t raise their eyebrows, they don’t roll their eyes, they don’t show any attitude, they don’t answer back. This is how Isma’il was — which is why, when Ibrahim told him he had to slaughter him, he said: “Ya abati-f’al ma tu’mar” — O my father, do what you have been commanded.

Look at the contrast: the father of Ibrahim was so intolerant that he said, “You go, I don’t want to see you, if I see you I’m going to kill you.” And Ibrahim asked Allah for righteous offspring, and Allah gave him such a righteous, obedient, patient child. Allah gave him not just one son but also Ishaq, and Ibrahim said: “Alhamdulillahi-lladhi wahaba li ‘alal-kibari Isma’ila wa Ishaq. Inna Rabbi la Sami’ud-du’a” — all praise is for Allah, who bestowed upon me in my old age Isma’il and Ishaq. Indeed, my Lord surely hears du’as.

Ibrahim did not become a father at a young age; he became a father at a very old age. It is possible he made du’a when he was younger, and his du’a was fulfilled many years later. And look at what he says: “Indeed my Lord surely hears du’as.” Do we say this about Allah? If we have been praying for something for five years, ten, fifteen, twenty — do we say, “Inna Rabbi la Sami’ud-du’a”? Unfortunately, a lot of times people say things like, “My du’a is not heard, Allah doesn’t hear my du’a, Allah doesn’t give me what I’m asking for.” We should not say these kinds of things about Allah.

Illustration used in the lesson

Parents know what they should and should not give their children. Sometimes children are very eager that their parents get them a cell phone — a child turns thirteen or fourteen, and some even at the age of ten start asking for their own phone, their own laptop, their own computer, their own iPad. Do parents fulfil every wish? No. Why? Because they know this is not the right time. It is not that they are saying they will never get it — but at a time that is better, when they know their child will be able to use it properly. Allah knows us better than our parents know us, better than we know ourselves. So believe in the timing of Allah. Allah is never late; His timing is perfect.

And Allah answered Ibrahim’s du’as so beautifully that He not only gave him righteous children — He made him the father of prophets. All of the prophets after him came from his progeny.

Ya’qub (‘alayhis salam)

Ya’qub loved his son Yusuf. His children threw Yusuf into a well and lied to their father that a wolf had eaten him. His response was: “Fa sabrun jameel, wallahul-musta’anu ‘ala ma tasifun” — so beautiful patience is what I will observe, and Allah is the one whose help is sought against what you describe. And later he said: “Innama ashku baththi wa huzni ilallah” — I complain of my grief and my sorrow only to Allah.

And his du’a was accepted. There came the day when the bearer of good news came and brought him the shirt of Yusuf. Ya’qub had become blind — he lost his eyesight because he wept so much for Yusuf, and probably also because he was very advanced in age by then.

Yusuf (‘alayhis salam)

Yusuf was in another kind of difficulty, where the women were coming at him and wanted him to do evil. What did he do? He asked Allah: “Rabbi-s-sijnu ahabbu ilayya mimma yad’unani ilayh” — O my Lord, the prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me.

There are some people praying, “Get me out of prison.” Yusuf was praying, “Get me into prison.” Everyone has different needs, different desires, different goals, different ways of thinking. Allah is able to give you the opposite of what He has given someone else. It is not that Allah is only able to do one thing — He is able to do all things, and to give you what you are in need of.

Musa (‘alayhis salam)

When Musa accidentally killed a man and the people were plotting to kill him, he had to flee Egypt. On his way towards Madyan he said: “‘Asa Rabbi an yahdiyani sawa’as-sabeel” — I hope that my Lord will guide me to the right path. He is fleeing as a refugee, empty-handed and unprepared — and in that condition he places his hope in Allah and asks Him for guidance.

When he reached Madyan, imagine his condition: tired, afraid, not knowing where he was going to sleep, what he was going to eat, or what his future would be. And in that condition, when he saw two women struggling with their flock, he got up and helped them. Imagine if in a condition like that someone asked us for water — we would become so impatient, so angry, so irritated. Then he made du’a: “Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir” — O my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send my way. And Allah accepted his du’a: he got not only a home, but a job, a wife, and security.

Musa continued to call upon Allah at every stage. When Allah granted him prophethood and sent him to Fir’awn, he prayed: “Rabbi-shrah li sadri, wa yassir li amri, wahlul ‘uqdatan min lisani yafqahu qawli,” and he asked for a helper from his family — specifying Harun, his brother. And Allah said: “Qad utita su’laka ya Musa” — you have been given what you asked for. Harun was made a prophet and his helper, and together they went to Fir’awn.

Note that the mistake Musa made was an accident — it was not intentional. But he recognized it as something wrong, and he asked Allah for forgiveness, for guidance, and for goodness, and Allah gave him so much. Contrast this with the hypocrites: when they were called to the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam so that he would seek forgiveness for them, “lawwaw ru’usahum” — they turned their heads away arrogantly and said they did not need it. That is arrogance. The prophets of Allah were so humble; they admitted their errors.

Zakariyya (‘alayhis salam)

He was old and had no children, and he looked at the condition of Bani Isra’il and realized there was no one among them in whom he could place hope to lead them, to command what is right and forbid what is wrong. So he called upon Allah: “Rabbi la tadharni fardan wa anta khayrul-warithin” — O my Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors. And Allah says: “Fastajabna lahu, wa wahabna lahu Yahya, wa aslahna lahu zawjah” — We answered him, and bestowed upon him Yahya, and We reformed for him his wife, because she had been barren before that.

Sometimes fertility issues are so severe that people are basically told they cannot have a child, that it is not possible. Allah is able to do miracles. Allah is able to give you things through means, and also without any means, because indeed Allah is able to do all things.

The Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam

Look at how much he used to call upon Allah. If you look at any collection of prophetic prayers, how lengthy is that collection? There are du’as for all twenty-four hours of the day. When you wake up, there is a du’a. When he would wake for tahajjud, while sitting, he would recite the last ten verses of Surat Ali ‘Imran, and within those verses are many du’as. There is du’a for making wudu, before entering the bathroom, when exiting it. Salah is all du’a; after salah is du’a; between the sunnah and the fard there is du’a. There are adhkar in the morning, du’a for entering the market, du’a after eating, after wearing clothes. When you are in the habit of calling upon Allah, then you will call upon Him even in the most difficult circumstances, and even when you are in ease.

Hadith — the Battle of Badr

When the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam saw the army of the enemy and how many there were, he turned towards the qiblah, extended out his hands, and began calling upon Allah: “Allahumma anjiz li ma wa’adtani. Allahumma ati ma wa’adtani” — O Allah, accomplish for me what You have promised me; O Allah, give me what You have promised me. He continued so long that his mantle slipped down from his shoulders. Abu Bakr (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) came to him, picked up his shawl and put it back on his shoulders, then embraced him from behind and said: “O Prophet of Allah, this prayer of yours to your Lord will suffice you, and He will fulfil for you what He has promised you.”

And Allah did fulfil His promise. He says in the Qur’an: “Idh tastaghithuna Rabbakum fastajaba lakum” — when you were desperately calling upon your Lord for aid, He answered you. And Allah sent angels to help him.

Chapter Sixteen

The Righteous Who Called Upon Him

This was not only the way of the prophets. Even the righteous before us called upon Allah in their hardship, and Allah answered them. There are so many stories like that — the three men who got trapped in the cave, each one of whom made du’a, and Allah delivered them to safety.

The boy and the king

A boy was calling people to Allah, and the king sent his men to kill him — to take him to the top of a mountain and throw him down. When they reached the top, the boy said: “Allahumma-kfinihim bima shi’t” — O Allah, suffice me against them with whatever You want. And there was an earthquake, and all of them fell except the boy. The king tried again, sending him with his men to the sea, telling them to throw him off the ship in the middle of the water. And again the boy prayed the same words — and there was a storm, and all of them drowned except for the boy.

Asiyah

Fir’awn had tied her up in such a way that on both of her hands and both of her feet there were giant nails, like pegs, fastening her to the ground. She could not sit up, she could not walk away, she could not run away — and if she even tried to get up, it would hurt even more. And she called upon Allah: “Rabbi-bni li ‘indaka baytan fil-jannah, wa najjini min Fir’awna wa ‘amalih, wa najjini minal-qawmiz-zalimeen.” And Allah showed her her home in Jannah. Allah fulfilled her du’a.

Sarah, the wife of Ibrahim (‘alayhis salam)

The king captured her and wanted to be intimate with her. For a woman this is extremely hard — sexual assault is traumatic, it can cause PTSD, it is a crime, it is a form of great violence against a woman. What did she do in that condition? She made du’a to Allah: “Allahumma in kuntu amantu bika wa bi rasulika wa ahsantu farji illa ‘ala zawji, fala tusallit ‘alayyal-kafir” — O Allah, if I have truly believed in You and in Your Messenger, and I have guarded my chastity except with my husband, then do not let this disbeliever have power over me. As the king tried to approach her, he felt paralysed. Sarah was afraid people would think she had killed him, so he got up — and again he tried to come to her, and again she prayed, and this happened multiple times. He was not able to touch her or harm her at all.

Khawlah

Her husband said very abusive words to her, words that were very damaging to their relationship, to their marriage. So she complained to Allah — and Allah revealed verses that brought a solution to her problem.

The woman with the goats and the spinning wheel

There was a woman at the time of the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam who had some goats and a spinning wheel, which she used to make yarn and earn her living. On one occasion she went out with the army to assist in whatever was within her capacity, and when she returned, her goats were gone and her spinning wheel was gone. So she called upon Allah: O Allah, You have guaranteed security for the one who goes out in Your way, and I have lost my goat and my spinning wheel — so I beseech You regarding them. And the following morning she got back her goat with another goat like it, and her spinning wheel with another one like it.

Sometimes what you want or need may seem very insignificant to someone else. If you found out someone was praying for a missing goat, you would laugh — a goat? A spinning wheel? It might not be significant to us, but it was something very important to her. So she called upon Allah, and Allah answered her.

Chapter Seventeen

The Sahaba and the Salaf

We can only call upon Allah when we know that du’a is the strongest resource we have, the most effective way of helping ourselves.

When ‘Umar (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) was the khalifah, the Muslim empire expanded a great deal, and there was victory after victory, conquest after conquest. Whenever he would send an army, he would say to them: you are not given victory because of your great numbers; rather, you receive help from up above — it is Allah who aids you, Allah who helps you. This was his way of telling his soldiers to make du’a and ask Allah for help.

Hasan al-Basri once mentioned the different types of people who recite the Qur’an. One of them, he said, is the one who recites the Qur’an staying up in the night, who remains thirsty in the day and controls his wishes because of the Qur’an — he wants to eat but doesn’t, because he is spending time with the Qur’an; he wants to lie down and relax, go somewhere, talk to his friends, but he doesn’t. He sits on his knees and remains in his place of worship reciting Qur’an and calling upon Allah. And he said it is because of such people that Allah keeps our enemies away from us, and because of such people that Allah sends rain on us. Because of their du’as, the entire community benefits.

Zubayr (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) and his son

Zubayr was going to a battle and had a feeling that he would not survive. So he called his son ‘Abdullah and told him: sell my property and pay off all of my debts — and if you are not able to pay them off, then seek help from my mawla. ‘Abdullah was startled and asked, “Who is your mawla?” He said: Allah. Allah is my mawla. ‘Abdullah said: by Allah, whatever difficulty I experienced in paying off a debt, I would say, “Ya Mawla Zubayr, iqdi ‘anhu daynahu” — O Mawla of Zubayr, pay off the debt of Zubayr — and whenever I did that, the debt was paid off so easily.

This is how we should call upon Allah: Ya Allah, You are my mawla, You are my guardian, You are my master; I need Your help, You help me with this, You take care of this matter for me.

Sufyan al-Thawri (rahimahullah), when he would make du’a, would say: “O You who loves the slave who asks You a lot” — meaning, of all Your slaves, You love the one who asks You a lot.

And we learn that some of the salaf would make du’a for every little thing. Even if they needed salt, they would make du’a. We think du’a is just for the big things, the big problems — no, even for the little things. For example, you have an itch in your foot and you are not able to reach it because you are driving. At that time also, call upon Allah. For every little and big thing, ask Allah — and teach your children, remind your family, that they should also call upon Allah.

Chapter Eighteen

How Allah Accepts Du’a

When Allah accepts du’as, He accepts them in different ways. There are levels of acceptance. In a hadith we learn that Allah certainly accepts du’as as long as the slave does not become hasty — and to be hasty is that a person becomes impatient and gives up making du’a. So Allah responds; our job is to keep asking, to not despair, and to trust the way Allah chooses to respond.

Sometimes Allah gives us exactly what we prayed for — as with Ibrahim, who prayed “Rabbi hab li minas-saliheen” and was given good children. Sometimes Allah gives us something even better than what we prayed for. The wife of ‘Imran made du’a that she would dedicate her child to Allah, and she was hopeful it would be a boy — but it happened to be a girl. Having a girl was much better for her than having a boy, because that girl was Maryam, the mother of ‘Isa (‘alayhis salam). And sometimes Allah removes some hardship from us, or protects us against some calamity, because of our du’a.

Hadith

When a person makes du’a, Allah gives him one of three things: either Allah gives him what he prayed for, or Allah preserves the reward for him in the Hereafter, or Allah removes some difficulty from him because of that du’a — a difficulty in proportion to what he prayed for. The Sahaba said, “Then we will make a lot of du’a.” The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: “Allah has even more.”

So don’t think you have exhausted the number of things you can pray to Allah for. There is no limit. With the genie, there are three wishes — that’s it, and you cannot wish for more wishes. Of course, none of that is true, but these kinds of things are embedded in our heads; we are taught from the beginning that you cannot ask for a lot, that you only have three chances, two chances, five chances, and that’s it. But with calling upon Allah there is no limit. You can continue to ask Him.

And sometimes Allah makes our du’a a means of expiation for our sins — when we call upon Allah, He forgives our sins because of it.

Chapter Nineteen

The Arrogance of Not Asking

We should not be of those people who do not make du’a, because such people are called “alladhina yastakbiruna ‘an ‘ibadati” — those who are too arrogant to worship Allah. Du’a is worship, because Allah commands us to call upon Him; it is obedience. Those who do not call upon Allah are refusing, disobeying, showing arrogance. So not making du’a is arrogance, and there is nothing worse than arrogance.

And how can a person be arrogant and proud before the One who created him, brought him into existence, provides for him, gave him life, and will cause him to die? Imam al-Shawkani, writing about this kind of arrogance, says that pride is a form of insanity, a form of madness — that a person is too arrogant to make du’a to Allah, saying, “No, I am not going to ask Allah, I am self-sufficient. I am not going to make du’a because I don’t want to be disappointed. I am not going to make du’a because God doesn’t listen to me.” This is pride, and this is a form of madness. How can you be proud before the One who made you — before the One who gave you the ability to breathe, who gave you your brain, who gave you the capacity to do what you are doing, and who can take everything away from you in an instant? Pride is a form of ingratitude.

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that the weakest of all people is the one who is too weak to make du’a. So make du’a, and do not despair. We learn in a hadith that of the major sins is that a person despairs of relief from Allah and gives up hope of Allah’s mercy.

The Danger of Wanting a Quick Solution

Sometimes people become too impatient. They are making du’a, they are not seeing what they are praying for, and so they want a quick solution. They say, “Du’a takes too long, we want a quick solution” — just as if I have a headache, I swallow a pill and the headache is gone. So they ask: tell me what grave I can go to, what string I can tie, what spell I can read. These are all forms of shirk, of associating partners with Allah, and this is foolishness upon foolishness.

In the Qur’an we learn that those who rely upon other deities are like a spider which has made its home — and the house of the spider, the web, is the weakest of houses. Those who call upon someone other than Allah are relying upon something extremely frail and very weak. It is not going to help; it is not going to work. And we learn that none is more astray than the one who calls upon someone other than Allah — someone who will not respond at all, and who does not even have any idea that they are being called upon. When a person calls upon someone in a grave, they cannot even hear you; they cannot talk — that is why they are under the ground, they are buried. How can they hear you? How can they help you? If they could help you, they would first help themselves.

So never make that mistake of becoming hasty and wanting a quick solution by turning to someone other than Allah. Continue to call upon Allah.

And in these days of Ramadan, as you are fasting, continue to make du’a. When you break your fast, make du’a. In the night, make du’a. After salah, make du’a. Take advantage of these special times and call upon Allah.

Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar.
In the next session: the etiquette of du’a — the external and internal etiquette, the best times, and the best way of making du’a.
Chapter Twenty

Respond to Him, and Wait for His Response

Allah tells us that He is near and that He responds — and then He says, “falyastajibu li”, so let them respond to Me. How should we respond to Allah? It means we should obey Him, and it means we should talk to Him — because Allah commands us in the Qur’an, “Ud’uni”, call upon Me. When a person is in some difficulty, when they are feeling shame, when they are feeling guilt, when they are in need of something, they should not just sit like that. They should do something — and the best thing a person can do is call upon Allah: You forgive me, ya Allah; You guide me; You provide; You heal me; You show me the way.

But falyastajibu also means that they should hope for and seek a response from Allah — meaning they should not be hasty. Sometimes when we make du’a we want it fulfilled immediately, to see the result right away. Allah tells us here that they should seek His response, meaning they should wait for it and not become impatient. And look at the next words: “walyu’minu bi” — and let them believe in Me. Meaning they should trust Allah, His timing, His decree. We should expect the response from Allah alone.

Istijabah and Qubul

A lot of people think that if Allah responds to our du’as, this means He should give us exactly what we asked for. But there is a difference between istijabah and qubul. Istijabah is that Allah responds to our du’as — He answers, He does not ignore. Qubul is that He accepts the du’a exactly as it is.

So every du’a is mustajab — it is responded to, because Allah says “Ujibu”, I respond. Every du’a is answered, because Allah hears and Allah cares. But not every du’a is fulfilled in the way that you asked for.

Illustration used in the lesson

If a person is unwell and goes to the doctor and asks for a particular medication or a particular procedure, what will the doctor do? They will examine them, probably run some tests — but they will not necessarily give the patient the very medication or treatment the patient is asking for. The doctor will give what the doctor believes is best and right for the patient. And often the doctor prescribes something you never thought you needed, or sends you for a test you didn’t think you needed — and you accept it, because you recognize that the doctor knows better than you do, that their knowledge and experience is far greater than yours. If this is the case with human beings, then remember that Allah knows us better than we know ourselves, and He gives to the slave what is best for the slave.

Why Etiquette Matters

For any matter there is a proper procedure. If you are applying to a master’s programme, you don’t just fill out a form — you write something about yourself, you explain why you want to get into the programme, you seek good reference letters from your professors, you submit a resume demonstrating your work and experience. Why? Because you want to make your application strong, and the stronger the application, the greater the chances of acceptance.

Allah hears all du’as and responds to all du’as, and we should be certain of that because Allah Himself is telling us. But when we want our du’as to be given more importance, we need to invest more in them — and we do that by observing proper etiquette.

Consider salah: when you pray with iman, the salah counts. But in a hadith we learn that many people, when they pray, receive only a portion of the reward of that salah — a tenth of it, a fifth of it — because that reward is in proportion to their khushu’, their humility, their focus, their attentiveness. In the same way, if we want our du’as to be rewarded, to be effective, and to draw us closer to Allah — because the real fruit of du’a is closeness to Allah, and du’a is worship — then we need to observe certain etiquette, internally and externally. Internally: what is the state of our heart, what are the thoughts in our mind. Externally: our physical manner when we make du’a.

Chapter Twenty-One

Internal Etiquette: Tawhid, Sincerity, and Presence of Heart

1. Call Upon Him With Tawhid

The one making du’a should have belief in the oneness of Allah in his heart. Call upon Allah with yaqeen in His oneness: that Allah is One; that nothing happens without the will of Allah; that Allah is able to do all things; that everything is in Allah’s control; that Allah owns everything; that Allah created everything and everyone will return to Him.

When you have that in your heart and you call upon Allah, you realize that it is only Allah who can help me, only Allah who can grant me what I am seeking, only Allah who can give me the healing I want, only Allah who can guide the heart of my child, the heart of my spouse, my own heart, my friend’s heart.

And with this comes sincerity — that we call upon Allah alone. Allah tells us in the Qur’an to call upon Him making worship sincere to Him: your worship should be dedicated to Allah alone, your du’a should be dedicated to Allah alone, because you believe He is the only God, the only Rabb, the only one able to grant you what you seek.

2. Make Du’a With Attention and Focus

Our heart should be present and attentive — we should not be merely saying the words of du’a verbally; we should actually be asking. Sometimes we say the words and don’t even realize what we have said. In salah we ask Allah for forgiveness, we ask Him to send blessings upon the Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, we ask for protection from the punishment of Hell — but so often we are saying the words without actually asking, because our mind is elsewhere.

If someone is talking to you and it is obvious from their eyes or their hands that they are not really in the conversation — they are looking at their phone, and every few seconds they say “uh-huh, yeah, yeah, exactly” — you feel disrespected. You want them to be present, to be here. So the heart should be present when we are talking to Allah.

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: call upon Allah while being certain of being answered, and know that Allah does not respond to a supplication from the heart of someone who is heedless and occupied by play.

Sometimes we are saying our morning and evening adhkar while using our phone at the same time, not even thinking about what we are saying. We are asking Allah to protect our body, our eyes, our ears — and we are not even thinking about it, because we are busy swiping through photos or videos. This is not respectful. Be attentive; the heart should be present.

In a narration, one of the scholars was asked: do you not see how frequently people make supplication, and how rarely they are given what they ask for? He replied that this is because when many people make du’a they do so to show off, or their hearts are distracted — whereas Allah listens to the one who makes supplication firmly from his heart.

And part of this is that a person means what they are saying. Sometimes we say words of du’a without really meaning them. There are certain statements that have become so common in conversation — “may Allah give us this, may Allah give you that” — that people just say them without meaning them. So mean it when you are asking Allah for something.

Chapter Twenty-Two

Internal Etiquette: Conviction, Humility, and Privacy

3. Ask With Conviction

Ask Allah with the belief in the heart that Allah hears, that He gives, that He is able to give this to me and able to do this for me.

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that none of you should say, “O Allah, forgive me if You wish,” or “bestow Your mercy on me if You wish,” or “provide me with subsistence if You wish.” Rather, a person should be firm in his request, because Allah does what He wills and no one can force Him to do anything.

You don’t need to say “O Allah, give this to me if You wish” — of course Allah will only give it if He wishes; He does what He wants and no one can force Him. But on your part you should express yaqeen, conviction in the power of Allah and in the mercy of Allah, and your words should exhibit that.

4. Do Not Worry About Acceptance

We should not be preoccupied and afraid, wondering whether Allah will accept our du’a or not. One of the salaf used to say: I do not worry about the acceptance of du’a; I worry about du’a itself. Meaning our concern should be about making du’a — that I need to ask Allah; am I asking or not; how am I asking; am I asking enough. Your concern should be to make du’a properly, in the best way you can, with attentiveness — and then leave the results to Allah.

The moment you call upon Allah, the istijabah, the response, is guaranteed. How Allah accepts your supplication and how He grants it is up to Him. Your business is that you call upon Allah, so focus your attention on that.

5. Call Upon Him With Humility

The companions were travelling with the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, and every time they went up to a higher place they would raise their voices. The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: O people, be merciful to yourselves — you are not calling someone who is deaf or absent, but someone who is with you; He hears, and blessed is His name and exalted is His might. When you shout, that is the opposite of humility. So show humility in your manner and in your heart.

6. Express Your Need and His Favours

In du’a we should express our need and our dependency on Allah, and acknowledge His favours upon us. Consider the du’a of Zakariyya: O my Lord, my bones have become weak, my head is aflame with white — I am so weak, my body is frail, I have become old, and I am in desperate need. And he also showed gratitude: never have I been unhappy in my supplication to You, my Lord — I have always received something when I called upon You.

One of the scholars said that certain ingredients are necessary in du’a: that you express your neediness before Allah, that you show humility, that you show weakness and desperation, that you praise Allah the Exalted, that you acknowledge His favours, that you confess your sins, and that you make du’a with attentiveness and determination. When you do that, the du’a will be responded to.

7. Tadarru’ — Earnestness and Poverty Before Him

The Qur’an

“Call upon your Lord in humility and privately. Indeed, He does not like the transgressors.”

Tadarru’ is not only to lower oneself, but also to be earnest and insistent — to beg, and to manifest severe poverty before Allah. As you are making du’a, your face should show that you really want what you are asking for, that you are crying before Allah. Your face should not be the face of someone who does not care, or who is very distant, or who does not feel anything. Feel all of your emotions and express them — in your tears, in your face, in the manner that you are making du’a.

Remember how the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam raised his hands and kept calling upon Allah for so long that his upper garment fell down, and Abu Bakr (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) picked it up, put it on his shoulders, and consoled him.

8. Call Upon Him Privately

The Qur’an mentions private supplication. Call upon Allah privately — in your heart, or if you are saying the words with your lips, then in a way that other people around you cannot hear. You don’t always have to share with people what you are asking Allah for. There are certain goals, wishes, and things in your life that you share with people, but not everything. Certain goals and prayers should be kept private between yourself and your Lord. The person who knows and feels that Allah is near will call upon Him in private.

There are many benefits to private du’a. First, it shows that you believe Allah is near and that He hears — you don’t have to say your du’a out loud, because He hears you and He knows you. Secondly, it shows more respect. Think about it: if there is a king or a dignitary and you are speaking to them, will you shout? Will you be loud? In fact, when you love someone and have great respect for them, you want to spend time alone with them, to talk to them in such a way that no third person is there. So private du’a is more respectful, more humble, and more sincere.

Chapter Twenty-Three

External Etiquette: Wudu, the Qiblah, and the Hands

1. Making Du’a in a State of Wudu

Wudu is not a condition for making du’a or for its acceptance — but it is certainly mustahab, preferable. If a person is not able to make wudu before making du’a, there is nothing wrong with that; Allah still hears. However, when you make wudu and then make du’a, you will feel more attentive and closer to Allah, because the acts of worship Allah has legislated are a means of drawing close to Him. In a hadith we learn that the slave draws close to Allah by doing what Allah has commanded, and when he performs voluntary good deeds he draws even closer.

Hadith

Abu Musa came to the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam and mentioned that one of his companions had passed away, and that Abu ‘Amir had asked him to request the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam to seek forgiveness for him. The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam asked for water, and when it was brought he made wudu, then raised his hands and said: “Allahumma-ghfir li ‘Ubayd” — O Allah, forgive ‘Ubayd. He did not make du’a right there when he was given the message; rather he first made wudu, then raised his hands, and then made du’a.

You will experience this yourself: when you are in some difficulty, or you hear some news, or you feel very stressed, you go and make wudu and you feel calm, you feel closer to Allah. Then you raise your hands and make du’a, and you feel you have unburdened yourself — you feel relieved, because you have handed your matter over to Allah. When you make du’a you are entrusting your affair to Him. This does not mean that every time you make du’a you must first make wudu; it was not the habit of the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam to do so every time, but occasionally he did.

2. Facing the Qiblah

Again, this is not a requirement — it is just something better. We learn in various narrations that the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam made du’a while giving the khutbah, and a person giving the khutbah is not facing the qiblah; in fact their back is towards it. But in some narrations we learn that he made wudu, then faced the qiblah, and then made du’a.

In one hadith, the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam went to a certain place in Madinah, and when he reached it he asked for water, made wudu, faced the qiblah, and said: O Allah, Ibrahim was Your slave and Your friend — and he prayed for the people of Makkah for blessing — and I am Muhammad, Your slave and Your messenger, and I ask You for the people of Madinah, that You bless them in their mudd and their sa’ as You blessed the people of Makkah. In fact he asked for double the blessing. So he did not just make du’a where he was; he first made wudu, then faced the qiblah, and then made du’a. Sometimes you can do that, but it is not a must.

3. Opening the Hands

Some people, when they make du’a, put their hands over their face, completely covering it. Some make a fist with one hand and place the other hand on it — that is also not from the sunnah. The correct way is that we open our hands: our palms should be open.

Hadith

Allah is shy, He is generous, and He is ashamed to turn away empty the hands of His servant when he raises them to Him. And the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said: when you make du’a to Allah, do so with the palms of your hands and not the backs.

So the hands should be open and raised. Some people don’t raise their hands at all — they just place them on their lap, or raise them only a little in front of them. Raise them up, at least to face level or slightly below.

Chapter Twenty-Four

How to Begin, and How to Word It

Another external etiquette is that when we make du’a, we begin with the praise of Allah, then we send salah upon the Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, and then we ask for what we are asking for.

Use Comprehensive Words

It is okay to make du’a at length, but we should use comprehensive words, because the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam liked al-jawami’ min ad-du’a — comprehensive supplication — and left other kinds.

For example, we learn that he asked Allah for Jannah: “Allahumma inni as’aluka-l-jannah” — O Allah, I ask You for Paradise. He did not ask: O Allah, I ask You for a house made of white pearls, with crystal on the right side of Paradise, with five levels, and on the first level this and on the second level that. He was comprehensive: he asked Allah for Jannah — because when you have Jannah, you will have in it whatever you desire.

And really the best way to make du’a is to use the words the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam used. One of the unique gifts he was given was jawami’ al-kalim — comprehensive speech, where a few words are composed of a great deal of meaning. So we can use his du’as for ourselves also.

Avoid Takalluf — Pretentiousness

Ibn ‘Abbas said: avoid the use of rhymed prose in making du’a, because I noticed that the Messenger of Allah salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam and his companions always avoided it.

Du’a is not poetry, where every word rhymes with the next and everything you ask for rhymes with the next. You don’t have to be super eloquent. This is not an assignment testing your ability to express yourself eloquently or at length. Call upon Allah from your heart, in the words of the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam or in your own — but be normal. Talk to Allah in a normal way; don’t be fake and pretentious.

Chapter Twenty-Five

I’tida — Exceeding the Limits

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that in my community there will be some people who will exceed the limits in purification and in supplication.

In wudu we are to wash our hands, face, and arms three times — but some people will not be satisfied with three times and will do more. That is a kind of exceeding the limits. And people will also exceed in supplication. Allah says: call upon your Lord with humility and in private; indeed Allah does not like those who exceed the limits. So exceeding the limits means doing the opposite of what Allah has told us — He tells us to ask with humility, so exceeding the limits would be to ask without humility; He commands us to call upon Him privately, so the opposite would be to be very loud, screaming and yelling.

Exceeding the Limits in Manner

A person shouting, or wailing. Crying in such a way that tears fall from your eyes, and there is a sound — as the companions could hear from the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, like the sound of bubbling water — or crying that is very silent, this is permissible. But wailing, crying noisily while making du’a, is exceeding the limits. Raising the voice, shouting, is also exceeding the limits. And making du’a in such a way that a person shows no emotion at all — not crying, not showing any weakness or humility on their face — this too is exceeding the limits.

Exceeding the Limits in Wording

As mentioned: a person saying, O Allah, I ask You for a castle in Paradise made of white pearls, with a fountain of chocolate, with this many floors and this many levels and this decoration.

From the salaf

‘Abdullah ibn Mughaffal heard his son saying, “O Allah, I ask You for a white castle on the right side of Paradise as soon as I enter it,” and going on and on. He said to him: my dear son, ask Allah for Paradise and ask Allah to protect you from the Fire — and that is sufficient.

Exceeding the limits in wording also includes asking for something that contradicts what is already established. For example, a person says: O Allah, make me a prophet — that is not going to happen, because the line of prophethood has ended. Or a person says: O Allah, do not resurrect me on the Day of Judgment — but Allah will resurrect those who are dead; if Allah created you and gave you life, He will give you death and bring you back to life. Or a person says: O Allah, give me knowledge of the unseen. These are all forms of exceeding the limits.
