Just because we are calling upon Allah does not mean we become illogical, or disrespectful, or that we begin to test the power of Allah. We should call upon Allah as slaves of Allah, as those in need of Him, as those who believe in Him.

Chapter Twenty-Six

Seek Forgiveness, and Begin With Yourself

Another etiquette is that when we call upon Allah, we acknowledge our sins, show regret, repent, and seek forgiveness.

Hadith

If somebody commits a sin and then says, “O my Lord, I have sinned, please forgive me,” then Allah says: My slave has known that he has a Lord who forgives sins and punishes for them — I have forgiven My slave his sins.

So seeking forgiveness should be a part of our du’a — as in the du’a: O Allah, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day of Reckoning.

And this shows us another etiquette: when we make du’a for others, we should begin with ourselves first. In that du’a of Ibrahim (‘alayhis salam), what did he do? He first asked Allah to forgive him, then his parents, then the believers. So ask first for yourself, then for those who are closest to you and most deserving of your du’a, and then so on. It is reported that whenever the Messenger of Allah salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam mentioned someone and made du’a for them, he would first begin with himself.

Chapter Twenty-Seven

Insistence, Frequency, and What Not to Pray For

Do Not Be Hasty

Being hasty for results means that a person abandons du’a — if they don’t see results right away they say, “This doesn’t work, forget about it,” and they stop. This is wrong.

Be Insistent — Repeat Your Du’a

How do we insist? By repeating the words of du’a. It was the way of the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, as Ibn Mas’ud reported, that he would make du’a three times. This doesn’t mean every single du’a must be made three times — but the things you really desire, the things that are heavy on your heart, the things you desperately want, repeat those multiple times; three times is sufficient.

Hadith

Whoever asks Allah for Paradise three times, Paradise says: O Allah, admit him into Paradise. And whoever seeks refuge from the Fire three times, the Fire says: O Allah, save him from the Fire.

And part of this insistence is that we continue to make du’a and do not give up. It was said that the one who continues to knock on the door, it is hoped that the door will be opened for him. When you really want to enter somewhere and the door is closed, you knock once and there is no answer — you will not just give up. If you really want to go in, you will keep knocking again and again until the door is opened. So the one who continues to call upon Allah, it is hoped he will be granted what he is asking for.

Take your time when making du’a; do not rush. Sometimes we think making du’a once is enough — no. If you are worried about an exam or a test you have to take, don’t make du’a for it once: make du’a after Fajr, then again after Dhuhr, then after ‘Asr, then after Maghrib, then after ‘Isha, then again in tahajjud. Make du’a today, and tomorrow, and the day after.

Be Frequent — In Ease as Well as Hardship

Hadith

Whoever wishes that Allah should respond to him during hardship and grief, let him supplicate plentifully when at ease.

Do Not Pray Against Yourself, Your Children, or Your Property

Sometimes when we get tired, overwhelmed, and exasperated, then in our frustration we begin to pray against our children or against ourselves. This is very wrong.

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam forbade this, saying: do not invoke curses on yourselves, do not invoke curses on your children, do not invoke curses on your servants, and do not invoke curses on your property — lest you happen to do so at a time when Allah is asked for something and He grants your request.

So be very careful. Sometimes we get so frustrated with all the housework that we start praying against the blessings Allah has given us. We say things like: why did I have to have such a big house, I wish I had a smaller house, I wish I had fewer things, I wish I had fewer responsibilities. Be very careful.

Allah tells us that the human being calls upon Allah for evil the way he should be asking for good — and the reason is that the human being is very hasty, very impatient.

Do Not Pray for Sin or for Severing Family Ties

In a hadith we learn that du’a is granted as long as the slave does not pray for something sinful or for the severing of family ties, and as long as he is not hasty. For example, if a woman prays that her husband should not meet his mother, or that he should not meet his brothers — this is praying for the severing of the relationship between a mother and her child. This is wrong; this is not permissible.

Chapter Twenty-Eight

Wasilah — Permissible and Impermissible Means

Allah tells us in the Qur’an to seek wasilah to Him. Wasilah means to attain nearness and closeness to someone. So when we are making du’a, we should do and say things that bring our du’a closer to acceptance. This means two things.

1. Do Something That Draws You Closer to Allah

Before making du’a, perform a good deed: make wudu, pray two rak’ahs, give sadaqah, praise and glorify Allah, send salah upon the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam — and then ask.

2. Say Things That Increase the Chances of Acceptance

Mention the names of Allah, because Allah says that to Him belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them. And mention the names that are relevant to what you are asking for: if you are seeking forgiveness, say Ya Ghafur; if you want guidance for your children, say Ya Hadi; if you are seeking healing, mention Ash-Shafi.

You may also mention your righteous deeds. In the hadith of the three men trapped in the cave, each one mentioned a good deed: one mentioned how well he treated his parents, and a particular incident where he gave his parents preference over his hungry, crying children, saying, “O Allah, if I did this for You, then bring me out of this difficulty” — and the rock moved a little. The second man mentioned one of his good deeds, and the third did the same.

Asking a Righteous Person to Make Du’a

There is nothing wrong with requesting a righteous person to make du’a for you. People would come to the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam and request him to make du’a for them.

‘Umar (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) and the drought

When ‘Umar was khalifah there was a drought, with no rain for a very long time. So he requested ‘Abbas (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) to make du’a for rain, and he made du’a himself, saying: O Allah, we used to ask our Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam to invoke You for rain and You would bless us with rain; and now we ask his uncle to invoke You for rain.

Notice what ‘Umar did not say: he did not say that we seek nearness to You through Your Messenger — because the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam had passed away. Rather, he asked a righteous person who was alive at the time to make du’a. So it is permissible to ask someone righteous to make du’a for us — but we cannot request the dead, or mention them in our du’a as a means. This would be an impermissible wasilah, and Allah has forbidden it: in the Qur’an we learn that the mushrikeen would say that they only worship these deities in order to draw closer to Allah.

Sadly there are many Muslims who think their du’a will only be accepted if they mention that they beseech Allah through the wasilah of His Messenger. This is not correct. The Sahabah did not do that; the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam did not teach that — in fact he taught the opposite, and the Qur’an teaches the opposite: call upon Allah directly.

And while it is permissible to ask someone else to make du’a for you, what is not correct is that you don’t make du’a yourself and only ask other people to make it. Some people have this habit — they keep asking others, “Make du’a for me, make du’a for me,” but they don’t make du’a themselves. Make du’a yourself, and the du’a you make yourself should be more than your requests for others to make it for you.

Chapter Twenty-Nine

The Times When Du’a Is Answered

There are certain times when the chance of acceptance is greater:

  • Between the adhan and the iqamah — the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that du’a at this time is not rejected. Sometimes there are five or ten minutes before the iqamah; that time is very precious.
  • After salah — when he was asked which supplication is most likely to be listened to, he said: during the last part of the night, and at the end of the obligatory prayers.
  • In sajdah — in salah, or after salah; you can go into sajdah and call upon Allah in that position.
  • The last third of the night — the time of suhoor. When you are up anyway these days to eat, wake up five or ten minutes early. If you pray witr at that time you can make du’a with it; and if you have already prayed witr, then at least spend a few moments in du’a, because Allah invites us at this time and says: is there anyone who will ask Me, that I may give him?
  • The month of Ramadan — in a hadith we learn that in every day and every night of Ramadan people are freed from the Fire, and there is a du’a that is answered in every day and night of Ramadan.
  • The day of ‘Arafah.
  • When rain is falling.
  • When a person is in difficulty.
  • When drinking Zamzam — the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for, so make du’a before or right after you take a sip.
  • After the recitation of the Qur’an.
  • When you hear the crowing of roosters — ask for Allah’s blessing, because they have seen an angel.
  • When visiting the sick or the deceased — supplicate for good, because the angels say ameen to whatever you say. So when you go for the janazah, say something good and ask for good.

People Whose Du’a Is Answered

  • Those striving in the way of Allah.
  • Those going for Hajj and ‘Umrah — in a hadith we learn they are a delegation to Allah, His guests; He invited them and they responded, so when they ask Him, He will give them.
  • The one who is oppressed.
  • The traveller.
  • The father for his child — mothers make du’a anyway; mothers are overly concerned about their children, they forget themselves and are always preoccupied with every single one of their children. But fathers are typically busy thinking about work, business, and money outside the house, and in the way many cultures are, fathers are very disconnected from their children. A father should make du’a for his child. So when you see something in your children that you are praying for especially, remind the father of that child to make du’a.
  • Children who make du’a for their parents.
  • Du’a for someone who is absent.
  • The person who is fasting, until they break their fast — and at the time they break it.
  • Those who remember Allah a lot.
  • A just ruler.
  • The person who makes wudu, remembers Allah, and goes to sleep — and then, if he wakes in the night and makes du’a, that du’a is accepted.

Those Whose Du’a Is Not Accepted

Those who do not believe in Allah — because they are not calling upon Allah, they are calling upon something or someone else. Allah tells us the du’a of those who disbelieve is only in error.

In another narration we learn that when people do not command what is right and do not forbid what is wrong, there comes a point where they call upon Allah and He does not give them what they ask for, because He is displeased that they do not care about what is right and wrong. And in another narration we learn about the one who commits zina, that their du’a is not honoured — for why should Allah give them what they are asking for when they have put themselves so far from His mercy?

This does not mean that if a person is committing a sin, or has committed a sin, they are not worthy of calling upon Allah — they should. But they should first recognize their sin, make tawbah, seek forgiveness from Allah, and admit their sins. In this way they draw closer to Allah, and then they call upon Him.

So we should be eager to call upon Allah, and we should observe this etiquette — internal and external — when calling upon Him.

Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdik.
In the next sessions: the words of praise and glorification with which we begin our du’a, then sending salah upon the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, and then the du’as related to different themes.
Chapter Thirty

Ease Is Entirely in His Hand

It is one of the huge blessings of Allah upon His slaves that He removes hardship from them and makes things easy for them — and not only that, but He guides them and grants them ease in their matters, so that they are able to do the little and the big things. Because when a person has ease from Allah, when things are facilitated for them, only then are they able to do what they would not be able to do otherwise.

Consider even this: that you are able to listen to this lesson right now. Allah enabled you to have an internet connection, a device that runs the programs you need, the health and the ability to listen and follow along and focus, the freedom and the time in your life, and the ability to make this a priority right now. Anything we do, whether big or small, worldly or religious, we are only able to accomplish with the help of Allah — only when Allah makes it easy for us.

Ease is a huge favour of Allah, and we realize how huge it is at the times when we don’t have it — when things are difficult, when we are tested with hardship. Ease is not available at all times; it is not always guaranteed, not always granted to a slave as much as he would like. But when Allah puts us in difficulty, then we realize what a favour ease is.

As Shu’ayb (‘alayhis salam) said: “And my success is not but through Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I return.” If I am able to do anything, big or small, it is because Allah gave me the tawfiq — He gave me the opportunity, the ability, the enabling. And for the future I put my trust in Him: not in myself, not in my means, not in my resources. I turn to Him for help, for ease, and for the acceptance of my efforts.

It is not in your control to make matters of deen or dunya easy for yourself, or even for someone else. If your child is suffering from a headache or some pain, yes, you can offer some comfort food, perhaps some pain relief, perhaps an ice pack or a heat pad — but you cannot take the pain away. Only Allah can remove that pain. You cannot tell them to be patient; only Allah can enable your child to have sabr. Ease is entirely in the hand of Allah. He is the one who makes things possible.

Every single human being is tested with hardship, and each person is tested differently — children in one way, adults in another, mothers in one way, fathers in another, employees and employers each in their own way. And typically, when things get tough, we get stressed out; and as we get stressed, we snap, we lose our composure, we begin to panic, or we begin to doubt ourselves, or we begin to doubt Allah. The right way of responding to difficulty is to turn to Allah — He is the one who can make things possible; ease is in His hand.

Chapter Thirty-One

With Hardship Is Ease

Yes, there is difficulty and hardship in life — but along with it there is also ease. If one thing is difficult for you, at the same time Allah has made something else easy for you. If you are facing difficulty in one aspect, there is certainly ease in another. And what is also promised is that after hardship there is ease. Allah mentions both facts in the Qur’an.

The Qur’an

“Allah shall make after difficulty ease.” And: “Inna ma’al ‘usri yusra” — indeed, with hardship is ease.

The first means that the difficulty you are in right now is not permanent. Every difficulty of this world is temporary; it is going to come to an end, it is going to pass, and after it there will be ease and relief — because the darkest night also comes to an end, and the harshest winter also comes to an end.

And the ulama say that “with hardship is ease” means that with every hardship there is double ease — the ease is double that of the hardship you are experiencing at the moment. If you examine any challenge in your life: yes, the difficulty is real, it is not imaginary, it is there and it is very painful and can be incredibly hard. But Allah has not just put you in difficulty; He has also given you ease at the same time, and that ease is double the hardship. If we viewed our trials this way it would be so much easier to deal with them. Our difficulties become harder on us because we blow them out of proportion and magnify them — by focusing entirely on them and not looking at the ease Allah has created, or the ease He has promised.

Relief Comes at the Peak

Allah mentions about His messengers in the Qur’an that things got so difficult for them that the people they were sent to began to think they had been lied to — that these could not really be messengers of Allah, because they saw them tried so severely. But then, Allah says, Our help came to them.

Sometimes difficulty becomes so intense that you begin to wonder whether there is any end to it, whether things will ever get easy, whether there is now only ruin ahead — and the help of Allah comes right at that time. Compare this to the darkness of the night: at the beginning of the night, at the time of Maghrib, there is darkness but also some light; as the night continues the darkness intensifies and deepens, until there comes a point where it is completely, pitch dark — and then light comes in and the darkness slowly begins to fade. Darkness fades after it has reached its peak. This is often how illness is too: the symptoms reach their peak, things get really hard, and then comes relief.

Allah tells us in the Qur’an that He is the one who sends down rain after they had despaired — after people begin to give up hope, after things got really hard. So when things get incredibly hard, that is actually a good sign: a sign that what is next is ease, what is next is relief.

Chapter Thirty-Two

The Youth of the Cave: Effort and Prayer

The Qur’an — Surat al-Kahf

“Rabbana atina min ladunka rahmatan wa hayyi’ lana min amrina rashada” — Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy, and prepare for us from our affair right guidance.

These young men had fled their hometown because they believed in Allah alone, while the king of the time was an idolater who forced his people to worship idols and would execute anyone who left his religion. They did not want to be on the false religion of their king; they wanted to cling to the worship of Allah alone. And when they realized there was no way of surviving in their hometown, they knew they had to flee. They planned to meet at a cave, and they took refuge there — similar to how the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam and Abu Bakr, when they left Makkah, first hid in a cave and then took a different route to Madinah.

In the cave they asked Allah for two things. First, His mercy — and the rahmah of Allah includes every good thing: food, safety, calm, the removal of anxiety, rest, sleep, any good thing. They asked for special mercy, mercy from Him specifically — they were asking for extraordinary help, a great help, because their situation was extraordinary. This shows us that when we are in a very unusual, very tight situation that we have never experienced before, that is not typical at all, at that time we should expect extraordinary help from Allah — help that is not typical. We should have yaqeen that Allah is able to do the unusual in order to bring ease; He is able to do miracles.

Secondly, they asked for right guidance in their affair — that Allah guide them to the right course of action. Because when a person is in difficulty, sometimes their anxiety and fear cloud their thinking. They are not able to judge correctly, and out of haste or impulse, in a heightened emotional state, they are not able to think clearly. They become impulsive and hasty, or they begin to give up. So they asked Allah to guide them.

The Blueprint

Shaykh al-Sa’di writes that in order to find ease in their matter, these youths did a number of things. First, they went to a place where they could actually hide from the king — they did not just stay in danger doing nothing to help themselves. They left the place of danger, found a cave, and realized they could find safety there. They did what was in their capacity; they used the means available to them. Secondly, after putting in their effort, they put their trust in Allah — not in themselves or in any other creature — and they asked Allah for help.

And when they combined effort and prayer, Allah granted them special mercy: He caused them to sleep, took their fear and worry and anxiety away, and caused them to sleep for a very long time, so that by the time they woke and returned, that king was gone, that oppression was gone, that era was over. And Allah showed them the right course of action — because in that situation it was not right for them to use violence or be confrontational; it was in their best interest to avoid confrontation, to hide and protect themselves.

So this is the blueprint. First, do whatever is in your capacity. Don’t just sit there doing nothing, waiting for the help of Allah to fall from above. Yes, Allah’s help comes from above — but you also need to do what is in your capacity. Allah has made you capable, and He has put you in this test to see what you do. He did not put you in this test so that you sit idle and expect things to happen on their own. Secondly, along with your effort must be a great deal of du’a — that you humble yourself before Allah and call upon Him. When you call upon Allah, this shows you are putting your trust in Him, not in yourself or in your plan.

Chapter Thirty-Three

Why Allah Puts Us in Hardship

Allah created us for His worship, and in order to test us — to see which of us is excellent in deeds. In difficulty and in ease, what is it that we choose to do? Changing circumstances reveal our true self. So Allah changes our circumstances from ease to hardship and hardship to ease, to bring our true self out.

Allah tells us in the Qur’an: did you think you would just enter Paradise like that, while Allah has not yet known those who strive among you and those who are patient? Allah will certainly test you, to distinguish those who strive from those who don’t, and those who are patient from those who are not. So in life, tests are inevitable; hardship is a given.

The Qur’an

“And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits — but give good news to the patient.”

There are days when you are able to eat well at suhoor and keep a fast without really getting hungry — and there are days when you miss suhoor and fast on an empty stomach. There are days when you get the best, most delicious iftar, and days when you get a cold meal or food you don’t enjoy and stay hungry because you don’t feel satiated. Allah is testing you through this: how do you respond, how do you behave with those around you, how do you respond to Allah?

And loss of the fruit of your labour: sometimes you work on something for so long, waiting for the fruit of your effort, only to find that the fruit was ruined, that something happened because of which you don’t get to enjoy the result of your hard work.

But Allah says: give good news to those who are patient. Good news of what? Of what is coming up ahead. If someone has just suffered a loss, you would think good news is a kind of mockery — but no, this is hope: you are in hardship right now, but rejoice over what is ahead. This means that by definition, hardship for the believer is meant to bring what is good and better in the future — and that good may be in this world or in the next. One day you miss suhoor and are hungry all day, but then when you get to eat a delicious, satisfying meal at iftar, doesn’t that bring you so much delight and comfort and joy?

But note: Allah says give good news to those who are patient — not to those who are tested. Because everyone is tested, but not everyone is patient. The good reward is promised to those who are patient. And who are they? Those who, when some difficulty strikes them, say: “Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un” — we belong to Allah, and to Him we return. I belong to Allah, and the owner is the one who looks after his property and ensures it does not go to waste. And this means the difficulty is not going to last forever: after the difficulties of the world is the relief and joy and ease and blessings of Jannah. Those who say this are the ones who receive blessings from their Lord, and mercy — and salawat, meaning that Allah mentions them in a positive way before His angels. And they are the rightly guided. Those who are not patient are not guided in their hardship; their hardship overcomes them, they are not able to think clearly or act properly, and they only get themselves into greater hardship.

Ease Is a Test Too

Some people think that if I am a Muslim, if I believe in Allah and love Him and worship Him, then I should be protected against the hardships of this world. It is actually the reverse: when you say “I believe,” Allah tests the sincerity and the strength of that claim. And Allah tests us not only with what we find hard and difficult, but also with ease. Difficulty appears to be a trial because it is inconvenient; but ease is also a trial, and we forget that it is a trial because it is convenient — it brings us joy or happiness or benefit, so we don’t think of it as a trial.

Hadith

The magnitude of the reward is in proportion to the magnitude of the affliction. When Allah, who is Great and Glorious, loves a people, He puts them in hardship; those who accept it gladly receive Allah’s good pleasure, and those who are upset and displeased receive Allah’s displeasure.

Allah tests His slaves in order to raise their levels and ranks, to purify them, to bring them benefits. Whoever Allah intends good for, He puts that person in difficulty. We think that if Allah wants good for us we should be immune to hardship — it is the opposite, because there are so many benefits you get through difficulty that you cannot get through ease.

So when you are in difficulty, that means Allah wants something good for you. And when we say that those who accept it gladly receive Allah’s pleasure — how can you be happy with difficulty? You are happy with Allah, not that you are happy to have a fever. Who is happy when they have a fever? Who is happy with a headache? We are not expected to find joy in pain; we are expected to be happy with Allah in all circumstances — not angry with Him, not asking “why did You put me in this difficulty,” but saying: ya Allah, I accept Your decree; this trial came to me with Your permission and Your wisdom, and I accept it.

The person who approaches trials with this mindset — Allah will grant them ease, acceptance, and patience, and eventually huge rewards, because Allah is pleased with them. But the person who is angry, impatient, annoyed, who complains about Allah and becomes irritable, is not able to think clearly, is not guided to the right course of action, destroys the rewards he had earned thus far, wastes his efforts, and wastes this excellent opportunity Allah provided him to earn good reward.

Chapter Thirty-Four

The Prophets Were Tested

When we look at the lives of the righteous and those closest to Allah, we see that all of the prophets were tested with some kind of hardship. Allah says: the messengers before you were denied, and they were patient over their denial and over the hurt they suffered, until Our help came to them.

  • Nuh — 950 years striving to convey the message of Allah to his people.
  • Musa — tested through Fir’awn, whose crimes are well known.
  • Ya’qub — tested through his beloved son Yusuf being taken away from him by his other sons, so he was tested in regard to all of his children.
  • Yusuf — tested through imprisonment, for a crime he never committed.
  • Ayyub — tested through loss of family, loss of wealth, and illness in his body; and Allah says: indeed We found him patient. In some narrations he suffered his illness for eighteen years.
The day of Ta’if

‘A’ishah asked the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam whether he had ever encountered a day harder than the day of Uhud, and he mentioned to her the day of Ta’if. Makkah was no longer safe for him — his uncle Abu Talib, who used to give him protection, had died. So he went to Ta’if seeking some cooperation, and he did not merely face rejection: people chased him out. It was not only embarrassing but painful and frightening and physically hurtful. Where was he supposed to go? What was he supposed to do?

And ‘A’ishah herself, beloved to the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, was hurt by the people when they slandered her of a crime she never committed, and the rumours spread so widely that people began to believe them. In her words, she said that even if she were to say she was innocent, they would not believe her, because they had heard the lies so much that her claim of innocence would not convince them. And so she said what Ya’qub said: “Fa sabrun jameel” — so patience is most beautiful.

So when a person is tested, it does not mean Allah does not like them, or wants evil for them, or is displeased with them. There are multiple factors behind a trial, but ultimately every trial in this world is good for you — because that trial will either lead you to turn back to Allah, to introspect, to look at your own shortcomings; it will make you a better person, a better worshipper; it will be a means of purification and of drawing closer to Allah. This does not mean we ask for trials. Rather, when we are experiencing hardship, we should seek ease.

Chapter Thirty-Five

Seeking Ease: Iman, Taqwa, and Tawakkul

1. Iman and ‘Amal Salih

Allah tells us that the one who believes and does righteous deeds will have an excellent reward, and that He will speak to him from His command with ease. Whoever does righteous action, whether male or female, while being a believer, Allah will grant that person a good life.

One of the scholars said that the outcome of obedience to Allah is success and goodness in this world and the next, and that the most fortunate among all creatures is the one furthest ahead in obedience and servitude to Allah — the success of the slave is in doing what his Lord ordered him to do and leaving what his Lord forbade him from. Ibn al-Qayyim said that Allah is the Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful of those who show mercy, and the Most Powerful of those who have power — and His approval can only be gained by showing obedience to Him. If you want His mercy, if you want His help, if you want His power to be with you and not against you, then this can only come through obedience.

2. Taqwa

The Qur’an

“Whoever is conscious of Allah, He will create ease for him in his affair.” And: “Whoever has taqwa of Allah, He will create for him a way out” — a way out of every matter that becomes constricted upon him.

3. Tawakkul

Allah says: whoever puts his trust in Allah, He is sufficient for him.

Ibn Rajab said that when a difficulty intensifies, the slave begins to despair of the creation, and no longer seeks them or turns to them for relief. For example: you are sick, you have a fever. You message a friend saying you’re not well — they don’t see the message; it doesn’t even show as read. You call your mother; she doesn’t answer. You call someone else; they don’t respond. You email your workplace to say you won’t be in, and nobody sees that email for a very long time. Hours go by and nobody reaches out to check on you — not because they don’t care, but because they didn’t even know, they didn’t realize you needed help. So as you wait on people, one after the other they disappoint you, and the difficulty intensifies and the pain gets harder — and then you turn to Allah.

When difficulty intensifies you give up hope of the creation and place your hope and trust in Allah, and your heart turns towards Him alone. Then you get to experience true tawakkul. Otherwise we say “I put my trust in Allah” — but we don’t truly experience it until we learn to give up hope of people.

Hadith

Whoever suffers from destitution and beseeches the people for it, his destitution shall not end; and whoever suffers from destitution and beseeches Allah for it, Allah will send provision to him sooner or later.

Relief is not in the hands of people; it is in the hand of Allah alone. If you put your hardships before people, your pain, your difficulty, your hunger, your poverty will not go away — because people are not able to give you anything unless Allah enables them. The help comes from Allah, so go straight to the source.

Recognizing How Ease Arrives

The relief of Allah comes in different ways — some tangible, some intangible; sometimes very apparent, sometimes hidden from us. If a person is ill, ease may come as good health, the illness going away. Sometimes ease comes in the form of becoming free of people, independent of them, detached from the creation — because difficulty teaches you that you should not put your trust in people but in Allah alone. And sometimes ease comes in the form of Allah helping you to be patient, so that your capacity to bear hardship increases: you have a greater capacity to deal with challenges, which means you will be able to do more in life. The fear of discomfort keeps us from moving ahead, but when we suffer hardship it teaches us that we are capable, that we can go forward with the help of Allah, that we can take on this challenge.

Hadith

The help of Allah comes with patience, and relief comes with affliction; and with hardship there is ease.

It was said that if hardship enters a hole, ease enters along with it. If something difficult enters your life, along with it there is also ease. For example, you are working on a document on your computer and strange glitches begin to appear and you cannot figure out what is happening — a problem has entered, but double ease has entered with it. This happens often: you ask someone to help you figure out what is going on, and in the process you learn something new that helps you do your work more efficiently and better than before.

And be certain that ease is near — it is not late. Sometimes help comes a little later than you expect, but it is not late; it is at the perfect time, because now you are fully ready for it. If things are working out and somebody teaches you a shortcut on your computer, you’ll never bother using it, because you are comfortable in your ways. But when you are in difficulty and something isn’t working, and then someone teaches you a shortcut or two, you will actually use them — because now you are ready for it, now you are welcoming that ease.

And the entire time you are waiting for relief is not time that is wasted — it is worship, and you are rewarded for it. Because while you are waiting, you are observing sabr, you are showing that you believe in the promise of Allah, you are placing your hope in Him.

Chapter Thirty-Six

Patience, and What Helps You Hold On

Seek the help of Allah especially through patience and prayer — not with impatience. And patience is not easy; it is of the matters requiring determination. You need to be determined to have sabr, to have composure, to be deliberate and intentional: I am going to have sabr.

When Ya’qub (‘alayhis salam) realized he could not do anything to get his sons to bring their brother back, he said: “Fa sabrun jameel” — beautiful patience is what I will observe — and it may be that Allah will bring all of my sons back to me. And because of his beautiful patience, Allah did bring all of his children back to him. This is how the help of Allah comes: through patience.

Three Things That Help a Person Be Patient

  1. Keeping the reward in mind. Remind yourself that there is good reward for sabr — this is delayed gratification.
  2. Waiting for the ease that is promised. You believe Allah has promised ease, so you expect it and wait for it and don’t give up hope. You know you are not going to fast forever — only until the sun sets. So when you know there are only a couple of hours left, you have patience: you check the clock and see five hours left, then three hours, then thirty minutes, then five minutes. Because you know it is going to end, you have sabr. In the same way, know that every period of hardship in your life has an end, and there is relief that Allah has promised.
  3. Gratitude. Repel the hardship with gratitude over present blessings and gratitude over past blessings. Start being grateful for what Allah has given you now, and for what He gave you before — and when you focus on the blessings Allah has given you, sabr becomes easy.

Strengthen Your Connection With the Qur’an

This can be listening to more Qur’an, reciting more, reflecting on it, memorizing, or reviewing what you have memorized — in whatever way, strengthen your connection with the Qur’an, because that brings ease. A pious man was asked how much Qur’an a person should recite every day, and he said: recite in proportion to the happiness and success that you wish for. If you want a lot of happiness, recite a lot of Qur’an; if you want a lot of success, recite a lot of Qur’an. And one of the salaf said: we got busy with the Qur’an, and the blessings of Allah and good things covered us.

Four Times Alhamdulillah

From the salaf

It was said: when I am struck by some difficulty, I praise Allah for it four times. First, I say alhamdulillah that it was not worse than it is, because it could have been worse. Secondly, I say alhamdulillah because Allah gave me the ability to be patient over it. Thirdly, I say alhamdulillah because Allah gave me the ability to say “inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un.” And fourthly, I say alhamdulillah because that difficulty was not in my deen — it was in my dunya.

Bring Ease to Others

Hadith

The one who alleviates the suffering of a believer from the sufferings of this world, Allah will alleviate his suffering on the Day of Resurrection. And the one who finds relief for someone hard-pressed, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah is in the aid of His slave as long as the slave is in the aid of his brother.

Sometimes when things get tough we think: I should stop caring about others and start caring about myself. I’m not going to help my mother, I’m not going to help my father, I’m not going to do this favour for my friend — I have to put myself first, so I’m going to say no to everyone and focus on myself. You can do that, but then don’t expect blessing in your life. Perhaps the help you have so far is because you are helping others, and if you stop, who knows — the little help you have may be removed entirely. And instead of blaming the people in your life for being a burden, blame yourself and check: do you have your priorities right? Are you giving Allah His haqq? Are you giving your parents theirs? Helping others is a way of receiving the help of Allah.

Chapter Thirty-Seven

What to Avoid, and What to Check in Yourself

Do Not Wail or Scream

In impatience, do not begin to scream and wail. The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam mentioned that this kind of sound is cursed. Imagine: a person is already in difficulty, and because of being unable to control themselves they show so much impatience that they begin to wail and scream — so they are inviting the curse of Allah rather than receiving His mercy, and things will only get harder and more unbearable for them.

Do Not Complain About Allah to People

Don’t complain to people that this is hard in my life and this and that, listing all your problems before them. Because when you do that, you are complaining about Allah — the one who allowed those difficulties in your life, who put you in all those hardships, whether personal, in your work, in your body, in your time, in your money.

Hadith

When a person is tested with illness and people come to visit him and he does not complain to them about Allah, then Allah promises him a good reward: that Allah will give him good health such that his flesh is replaced by better flesh and his blood by better blood, and the ability to do good deeds — or that Allah will give him better in the Hereafter.

Do Not Show Weakness

Weakness here means that a person begins to give up hope and stops trying hard. Do not stop trying; keep trying and do whatever is within your capacity. And increase in your gratitude.

Introspect — What Needs to Change?

When you are doing whatever is within your capacity to find ease, and you are praying and making du’a, and things are becoming increasingly hard or unbearable — do not blame Allah. This is the time to introspect, to check yourself: what do I need to change in myself in order to receive the help of Allah? Allah’s promise is true; He sends His help. The obstacle is on my part. There is something I am doing that is preventing His help from reaching me. So what is that barrier I am putting up, because of which I am repelling the help of Allah? Don’t blame Allah; check yourself — and if you are honest with yourself, you will find many things to change.

Perhaps, when hardship continues, you will finally make du’a properly rather than in passing or while rushing: you make wudu, face the qiblah, raise your hands, praise and glorify Allah, send salawat upon the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, make du’a, use wasilah by mentioning the names of Allah, perform good deeds, recite Qur’an, increase in dhikr. And perhaps you check yourself and see that your attitude with your mother is not the best — you are not spending enough time with her, not being kind, not giving her the attention she deserves — and so you change your behaviour. As you change, you become a better version of yourself. The difficulty is forcing you to become better, to set your priorities right, to pray salah in a better way, to be more consistent in your prayers and your dhikr, to seek more forgiveness.

The Qur’an

“As for he who gives and fears Allah and believes in the best reward — We will ease him toward ease.”

What is it that you have to give? That is not specified here, which means you can give whatever you can: showing obedience to Allah, praying more nafl, giving more sadaqah, spending in the way of Allah, doing good to people. The door is open; there is no limit. And fear Allah — this includes leaving sins, so check yourself: what words do I need to leave in my language? What behaviours do I need to change? What things displease Allah that are a major part of my life? And then keep reminding yourself that Allah’s promise is true.

Allah tells us that any difficulty you suffer is the result of what your own hands have earned; and that whoever turns away from the remembrance of Allah will have a constricted life. So check yourself: how connected are you with the Qur’an? How connected with salah? How often do you remember Allah?

Hadith Qudsi

“O son of Adam, make time for My worship — I will fill your chest with richness and remove your poverty. And if you do not do that, I will fill your hands with occupation and will not remove your poverty.”

So make time for ‘ibadah: the ‘ibadah of salah, of ‘umrah, of spending in the way of Allah, of helping the creation of Allah, of being good to your parents — because after the haqq of Allah comes the haqq of parents.

And when we make worldly things our ultimate concern, we learn in a hadith that poverty hangs before our eyes. Sometimes we are tangled up in problem after problem because we are obsessed with this world, our goals revolve around worldly goals, we are not concerned about the Hereafter — and Allah wants to shift our focus. So shift your focus from dunya to akhirah. And Allah says that the one who is stingy and thinks himself independent — who does not humble himself before Allah and denies the best reward, thinking that dunya is everything — such a person will be led towards difficulty, difficulty upon difficulty.

And make du’a for yourself. Don’t just continue to suffer and be in pain; raise your hands before Allah and ask Him for help. Sometimes we turn to people, we read book after book to figure out how to help ourselves — that is fine, you have to use the means at your disposal — but don’t forget to pray. The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that the weakest of all people is the one who is too weak to make du’a. And call upon Allah a lot in good times, so that your du’a in difficulty is also heard.

Increase in your dhikr: Allah tells the believers that when you face an enemy, be firm and remember Allah a lot, so that you may be successful. And in a hadith we learn that as long as a person is remembering Allah, Allah is with him. And seek forgiveness: Allah says, why do you not seek forgiveness from Allah, that you may receive mercy? So seek forgiveness especially while you are fasting, at the time you break your fast, in the night, and when you wake up.

Chapter Thirty-Eight

The Du’as for Ease

1. The du’a of the youth of the cave
رَبَّنَا آتِنَا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًا

Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy, and prepare for us from our affair right guidance. I need a lot of mercy from You, especially from You — and show me the way, tell me what to do, guide me to the best course of action.

2. The du’a of Musa (‘alayhis salam)
رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي

O my Lord, expand my chest for me, and make my affair easy for me. Because in difficulty, don’t you feel like your chest is getting constricted, like you cannot breathe? Especially if a person experiences anxiety or panic, they literally cannot breathe — you feel so alone, so constricted, so limited, so helpless in your difficulty.

3. The du’a of Yunus (‘alayhis salam)
لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنْتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ

There is no deity except You; glory be to You; indeed I am of those who are wrong. You did not do anything wrong; You did not make a mistake in putting me in hardship — I am the one at fault. So confess your mistake before Allah. And in a hadith we learn that when a person says this du’a, Allah will remove from him his karb, his affliction, whatever trial he is experiencing.

4. In worry, grief, illness, or any difficulty
اللَّهُ رَبِّي لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ

Allah, Allah is my Lord; I do not associate anything with Him. In a hadith we learn that whoever is afflicted by some worry, grief, illness, or any kind of difficulty and says this, Allah will remove that hardship from him.

5. The du’a for ease in every matter
اللَّهُمَّ لَا سَهْلَ إِلَّا مَا جَعَلْتَهُ سَهْلًا، وَأَنْتَ تَجْعَلُ الْحَزْنَ إِذَا شِئْتَ سَهْلًا

O Allah, there is no ease except what You make easy, and You make the difficult easy whenever You wish. Sahl is used for soft, smooth, level ground; hazn for rugged, hard ground. When you have to walk through rugged ground you get exhausted, maybe you get hurt, maybe you sprain your foot; it takes so long to cross a short distance. But ground that is smooth and level and open is so easy to traverse — you get so much done so quickly. So you are surrendering your matter to Allah: whatever I am finding difficult — whether an act of worship, or giving people their rights, or a bad habit I want to get rid of, or a promise I am not able to fulfil; whether financial, or in my marriage, or my children, or my employment or business; small, like being stuck in traffic, or big, like a major exam; or grief and sadness I am not even able to disclose to people — Allah is able to make it easy, because all matters are in His hand. Repeat this over and over again; it is an affirmation.

6. The words that create openness
لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ الْحَلِيمُ الْكَرِيمُ، لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ، لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ السَّبْعِ وَرَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ

There is no deity except Allah, the Ever Forbearing, the Ever Great; there is no deity except Allah, Lord of the Great Throne; there is no deity except Allah, Lord of the seven skies and Lord of the noble Throne. Here you are affirming the oneness of Allah and mentioning His perfect names and attributes. These are the words that create openness and vastness in your life. Sometimes you are working hard and not getting the promotion you wish for, or the increase in your pay; or you are applying to a programme and not getting acceptance anywhere; or you want work and are not finding it anywhere. When you find all the doors closed and want an opening in your life, say these words.

7. For a good outcome

O Allah, grant a good end to all our matters, and save us from humiliation in this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. Because in difficulty the outcome can be very painful and severe — so you are asking Allah for a good outcome in everything in your life.

8. From constriction

O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the constriction of the world and the constriction of the Day of Judgment. Whatever constriction I am experiencing right now — in my relationships, in my money, in my home — ya Allah, I seek refuge in You from it; and save me from the constriction of the Day of Judgment, bring me ease on that day.

9. The du’a at the end of a gathering

O Allah, apportion for us fear of You that shall come between us and disobedience to You; and of obedience to You that which shall cause us to attain Your Paradise; and of conviction that will make the difficulties of this world easy upon us. And grant us the ability to benefit from our hearing, our vision, and our strength for as long as we live, and make these faculties inherit from us — meaning, let us benefit from them until we die. And let our vengeance be upon those who have wronged us, and aid us against those who show enmity towards us. And do not make our affliction in our religion, and do not make this world our greatest concern, and do not impose upon us someone who will not show mercy to us.

Here we are asking Allah to protect us from afflictions in our deen — because when a person suffers a trial in their deen, that can actually lead them to shirk, can make them forget to worship Allah, can turn them toward hypocrisy and deceit and disobedience. How often it happens that because of poverty a person ends up committing crimes or theft; or a person is afflicted in his deen, so he thinks negative thoughts about Allah, and that leads to kufr and shirk. So we ask Allah to protect us from such trials — and that in any trial we do experience in this world, He helps us, especially when we suffer at the hands of people.

Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdik.
Chapter Thirty-Nine

Begin With Praise, Then Ask

The relationship between the slave and his Master is that we are beggars to Him, we are in need of Him, and He is ever generous, ever merciful to us. He is the one constantly giving us what we are in need of. He gives us when we ask, and He also gives us when we do not ask — in fact, there are more things He has given us without our asking than the things He has given us on our asking. And our needs are such that they never end; we are constantly dependent on Allah, constantly in need of His favours, His mercy, His generous bestowal.

We have learned in the etiquette of du’a that we should begin with the praise and glorification of Allah, then send salat on the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, and then ask Allah for what we wish, what we need, what we desire.

Glorifying Him Through His Names

You can glorify Allah by mentioning His excellent names and attributes. For example, you begin your du’a by saying Allahumma — O Allah. And the name Allah itself is very powerful, encompassing within it all of His names and attributes, because Allah means the God, the only one worthy of worship: the one perfect in His ability, the one who has knowledge of everything, the one who created everything, the one who is all wise.

Or you say Rabbana — our Rabb — or Rabbi, my Lord. The name Rabb contains the meaning of khaliq, malik and mudabbir: the creator, the master and owner, and the one who takes care of His creation, who provides and sustains. And you can also mention other names and attributes of Allah that are related to what you are specifically asking Him for.

Hadith

“O Allah, indeed I ask You, as I bear witness that there is no deity except You, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, nor is there to You any equivalent.”

Ibn Mas’ud (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) said that when a person intends to ask Allah for something, he should begin with the praise and glorification that Allah is deserving of, then send salat on the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, and then make du’a — because this makes it more likely that he will attain what he desires.

Hadith

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam once heard a man making du’a in his salah, and that man did not praise Allah and did not send salat on the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam. So he said about him: ‘Ajila hadha — this one has been hasty. Then he called the man, and said to him and to those present: when any one of you prays, he should begin with the glorification of his Rabb and praise Him, then invoke blessings on the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, and then supplicate Allah for anything he wishes.

Otherwise our du’a would be hasty. It would mean we are rushing, that we are being impatient, that we are just being greedy for what we desire. Whereas du’a is actually worship — a form of showing servitude to Allah — and the real fruit of du’a is that you attain closeness to Him. So if you rush through your du’a and just say, “O Allah, just give me this,” spending no time glorifying Allah, not repeating His name, then you are being hasty.

At the end of Surat Ali ‘Imran, many du’as are mentioned, and all of them begin with Rabbana. So sometimes, when you are making du’a, you can simply say Rabbi after every few words, or Allahumma — mentioning His perfect, beautiful names, because this is a form of glorifying Him.

Chapter Forty

What Surat al-Fatihah Teaches Us

In Surat al-Fatihah, Allah teaches us how we should worship Him and how we should call upon Him. We begin with the praise and glorification of Allah: all praise is for Allah, the Lord of the worlds, the extremely merciful, the continuously merciful; the master, the sovereign of the Day of Recompense. And then we say: You alone we worship, You alone we seek help from. Guide us to the straight path, the path of those whom You have favoured, not of those who have received Your anger, nor of those who are astray.

So the first surah of the Qur’an teaches us the adab of calling upon Allah: first begin with praise, and then ask. And when you recite it, bear in mind that Allah is Mujib — He responds. When you say Alhamdu lillahi Rabbil ‘Alameen, Allah says: My slave has praised Me. When you say Maliki Yawmid Deen, He says: My slave has glorified Me. When you say Iyyaka na’budu wa iyyaka nasta’in, He says: this is between Me and My slave, and My slave will have what he asks for. And when you ask for guidance, He says: this is for My slave, and My slave will have what he asks for.

We learn that you never recite a single letter of Surat al-Fatihah but that you are granted it — meaning you are granted its reward — and if you make du’a after reciting it, that du’a is also granted. The same is the case for the last two verses of Surat al-Baqarah.

Why We Begin With Hamd

Hamd is to describe someone with their most perfect attributes. Allah has the most perfect attributes; He is all good, meaning every name and attribute of His is excellent. The thing with the creation is that where they have good qualities, they also have some negative traits. Allah is Al-Hamid — ever praiseworthy, always perfect — so He is most deserving of praise. And hamd is not just to mention someone’s most perfect traits, but to do so with love, with respect, with adoration and with sincerity, knowing that the one you are praising is worthy of that praise. And it is only Allah who is like that.

Whatever blessing we have is from Allah — any worldly blessing, and even the blessing of guidance. In Surat al-Kahf: all praise is for Allah, who has sent down the Book upon His slave — meaning the revelation of the Book is a favour, a blessing to mankind from Allah.

Jamal and Jalal

Then we say Maliki Yawmid Deen: He is the sovereign of the Day of Judgment, the only one who will have power on that day. The entire creation will be powerless before Him. In this world Allah has given temporary power and ability to people, but on that day sovereignty will exclusively be for Allah alone.

And this shows us that we should remember not just the Jamal but also the Jalal — not just the beauty of Allah, but also His might. Sometimes we focus only on the names that mention His mercy, His love, His kindness, His generosity, His forgiveness, and that is good. But here Allah is teaching us that He is Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim and Maliki Yawmid Deen. So remind yourself that He is also Shadeedul-‘Iqab, severe in retribution, and Khabeer, fully aware of what we are doing.

So when you are making du’a, have in your heart that love and also ta’zim, respect. Bring to heart the perfect beauty of Allah and also His perfect might and greatness, and bring to your heart both hope and fear. Because sometimes people become a bit disrespectful before Allah when making du’a, where they begin to speak as though they are speaking to a child, or they begin to say things which are not appropriate, as if testing the power of Allah.

Worship Before Asking

Then we say Iyyaka na’budu wa iyyaka nasta’in. This is a form of wasilah. One of the forms of wasilah is that when we make du’a we mention something good we have done — not to show off, not to demand a reward from Allah, but because good deeds are a means of drawing closer to Him.

And this is so beautiful: first is ‘ibadah, and then isti’anah. First worship, and then seeking help. Sometimes we think we don’t need to be religious as long as we are spiritual — that we have a lot of love for God and a lot of hope in God and we praise Him, but when it comes to the commands He has given and the way He wants us to live our lives, we don’t want to do that. This is not the proper way. Allah is teaching us that first comes ‘ibadah and then isti’anah. So before you seek help from Allah, do something good: give some charity, make some dhikr, do some tasbih, send salat on the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam, recite some Qur’an, pray a nafl prayer — and then ask Allah for help.

Asking for Guidance, Always

Then we say Ihdinas Siratal Mustaqim. Surat al-Fatihah is a surah we recite in every salah, multiple times every day — and what we are asking Allah for in it is guidance. You would think that if you ask for something once that should be sufficient, but it is not, because we are always in need of guidance, every moment. In the first rak’ah we ask Allah for guidance, and a few moments later we ask again. This means we needed guidance a few moments ago, we need it now, and we will need it a few moments later, and after that, and after that.

One of the scholars said that people are in need of guidance more than they are in need of sustenance and other help. Because when a person has guidance, Allah will help them and Allah will give them sustenance — as Allah says, whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him from his troubles, and will give him sustenance from where he could not even expect. And who will fear Allah? The one who is guided.

So Surat al-Fatihah teaches us three things about calling upon Allah. First, that we should make du’a at all, because we are being taught to ask Him. Second, that we should begin du’a with the praise and glorification of Allah, just as Surat al-Fatihah begins with praise and glorification. And third, that we should use wasilah — first worship Allah, or perform some act of worship pleasing to Him, or mention it, and then make du’a.

Chapter Forty-One

The Way of the Prophet

salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam

He would also begin his du’a with the glorification and praise of Allah.

Hadith — his du’a on rising for tahajjud

O Allah, for You is all praise. You are the holder of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them. For You is all praise; You own the dominion of the skies and the earth and whoever is in them. For You is all praise; You are the light of the heavens and the earth. For You is all praise. You are the Truth, and Your promise is true, and Your meeting is true, and Your word is true; Paradise is true, the Fire is true, the Prophets are true, Muhammad salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam is true, and the Hour is true.

O Allah, to You I surrender, in You I believe, and upon You I put my trust. To You I return, with Your help I argue, and You I take as judge. So forgive me for whatever I have sent ahead and whatever I have delayed, and whatever I have done secretly and whatever I have done openly. You are the one who makes things go forward and others backward. There is none to be worshipped but You.

Praise at the beginning, praise at the end, and in the middle he asked for forgiveness. This du’a is so beautiful — there is so much praise and glorification of Allah in it. And what was he asking for? Forgiveness. He was asking for forgiveness when all of his sins were already forgiven, as Allah told us in the Qur’an. Yet he would seek forgiveness from Allah so beautifully.

So if we want to learn what the best and most beautiful way of worshipping Allah is, then his example is the best example for us. This is why we have been told that if you love Allah, then you should follow the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam — and when you follow him, Allah will love you.

And if you begin your tahajjud like this when you get up, of course you will feel closer to Allah. That is a time when Allah draws near His slaves and invites them to worship Him, to call upon Him, to ask Him. If you praise and glorify Allah like that, you will feel that love for Allah; you will feel closeness to Him.

Another thing we see here is that he praised and glorified Allah more than the words he used to ask Allah for something — the words of hamd were more than the words of du’a. And sometimes we can do that: spend more time praising and glorifying Allah and less time asking. Because when you praise and glorify Allah, He will forgive you your sins, He will guide you, and He will give you more than what you could ask for and more than what you could even imagine or think of asking Him for.

And we learn that on the Day of Judgment, the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam will glorify and praise Allah with words he will be taught at that time. He glorified and praised Allah so much here, yet on that day he will be taught special words with which to glorify and praise Him. So we should busy our tongues with the glorification and praise of Allah in general, but specifically when making du’a.

Chapter Forty-Two

Tasbih and Tahmid

Tasbih is to glorify Allah; tahmid is to praise Him. Tasbih is, for example, that you say SubhanAllah; tahmid is, for example, that you say Alhamdulillah.

Tasbih is that you are saying Allah is perfect — that He is free from any imperfection, any fault, any deficiency, any error, any resemblance to the creation, any partner or equal or child. That Allah is far above and beyond even the things people imagine about Him, and the false assumptions people have about Him. This is, in essence, what SubhanAllah means.

Allah instructs His Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam to glorify Him with His praise. Allah glorifies Himself: glory be to the one who took His slave on the night journey. The believers are told to glorify Allah in the morning and in the evening, at the two ends of the day. The heavens and the earth glorify Allah, and whoever is within them. The birds glorify Allah; even thunder glorifies Allah. The angels glorify Him, and the carriers of the Throne, the angels closest to Allah, glorify Him. When Dawud (‘alayhis salam) would glorify Allah, the mountains and the birds would join him. And it is because of tasbih that the creation is given sustenance, as we learn in one of the narrations.

These words are most beloved to Allah. So think about it: when you are making du’a and you begin with words that Allah loves, then instantly you are drawing closer to Him, you are inviting His mercy. We learn in a hadith that indeed your Lord loves hamd; and we also learn that there is nothing more beloved to Allah than praise.

Tasbih as Relief

Sometimes we are feeling very uncomfortable, very suffocated, or lonely in our thoughts and in our heads, and we begin to feel very negative because of what someone has said, or because of what we think someone is saying or doing. We feel so trapped in such negative thoughts. Sometimes there is some basis for thinking this way, and other times there is no basis — it is just imaginary. Regardless, when we are feeling like this we need to get out of that condition, and the way out is to call upon Allah. And sometimes you don’t even know what to ask Allah for. Then what should you do? Just start glorifying Allah.

In the Qur’an, Allah tells His Messenger salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam that certainly He knows that his chest feels constricted because of what people say. And think of the atrocious things people would say about him — such lies, such inappropriate things. Of course he would feel uncomfortable. What was the solution Allah gave him? Go respond to them, go refute them, busy yourself in answering them? No. Rather: glorify with the praise of your Lord, and be of those who prostrate. Busy yourself in tasbih and in sujud. When you do that, your heart will feel at ease, and Allah will take care of those who are talking against you.

Sometimes we feel very stingy with our money, afraid that we are going to have little left — a lot of people have to give in the month of Ramadan, and the thought of giving makes them afraid as they calculate what they have to give. Sometimes people have other fears, or there is general anxiety; these days every other person has some issue they are struggling with because of which they are anxious, afraid, worried. In a hadith we learn that whoever is afraid to spend his wealth, or is afraid of some enemy, or is frightened by the darkness of the night, should increase in tasbih — and in another narration, in tasbih and tahmid.

So tasbih and tahmid are not just a way of glorifying Allah. This is not just for Allah; this is for you also. You describe Allah’s greatness, you mention it — and that is what will fill you with light, that is the source of comfort for you, that is what will bring you relief. Because when you do tasbih you draw closer to Allah, and when you draw closer to Him you will receive His mercy, and that mercy will envelop you and will be a means of taking away your grief, your worry, your anxiety, your troubles.

Don’t underestimate the power of these words. In a hadith we learn that when you say tasbih, the space between the skies and the earth is filled up with reward. And sometimes our sins hold us back from calling upon Allah — what should we do then? Do tasbih, because when a person does tasbih their sins are forgiven even if they are like the foam of the sea. And when you say these words of praise and glorification, they ascend and revolve around the Throne of Allah as if making mention of you — because Allah says, remember Me and I will remember you. On the Day of Judgment these words will be heavy.

It was said that whoever constantly does tasbih, his face will become bright and he will constantly receive the blessings of Allah; and the one who constantly seeks forgiveness from Allah finds that the doors that were closed for him open up. And we learn that those who praise Allah will be the best of Allah’s slaves on the Day of Judgment.

Chapter Forty-Three

The Words of Praise and Glorification

So what are some ways in which we can glorify and praise Allah at the beginning of our du’a, and also in general? Every one of the phrases below is collected, with its Arabic, in the memorisation tracker at the end of this book.

SubhanAllah

Glory be to Allah. We learn in a hadith that if a person says this a hundred times before the sun rises and before the sun sets, then this is better for him than a hundred camels. Think about it: if you could get a hundred Teslas every day, you would do whatever was required — and if it were simply something you had to say, you would say it readily.

These days, in the time before iftar when you are laying the table and prepping and doing the last-minute things, busy your tongue with tasbih. And after Dhuhr, when a lot of people tend to take some rest, as you lie down, busy your tongue with the tasbih of Allah. These are words Allah has chosen; these are words Allah loves.

A man asked ‘Ali what SubhanAllah means, and he said it is veneration of the majesty of Allah — a way of glorifying Him, mentioning His perfect greatness. And when you say SubhanAllah, you are declaring the oneness of Allah; it is the basis of tawhid and a pillar of iman. And only Allah is deserving of tasbih, because He is the only one who is perfect, the only one who is ever living and will not die — people and jinn will die, all of the creation will die. So only Allah is worthy of such praise and glorification.

SubhanAllahi wa bihamdihi

Glory be to Allah, and praise is to Him. We learn in a hadith that these are words Allah has chosen for His angels — these are the words the angels say — and that this speech is the best and most virtuous speech.

When you say it, you are doing two things. First, by SubhanAllah you are negating anything negative, inappropriate or unbefitting from Allah, declaring Him free of all faults, above any imperfection, deficiency, error, similarity to the creation, or having an equal. Secondly, by wa bihamdihi you are affirming His most perfect traits. So this is complete and perfect praise: on the one hand you negate anything unbefitting, and on the other you affirm those traits which are befitting, which Allah is worthy of. This is real tawhid — our Lord is free of any fault, and He is perfectly good, He is all good.

Sometimes there are negative thoughts we may have about Allah. At those times, say these words: no, my Lord is perfect, He is always praiseworthy, He is always good; He has not made a mistake, He has not done anything wrong, He has not been unjust.

SubhanAllahi wa bihamdihi, SubhanAllahil-‘Azim

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that these words are light on the tongue, heavy in the scale, and beloved to Allah — an easy way of earning reward from Allah, an easy way of earning His approval. And Al-‘Azim is the one who is ever great: so great that our intellect, our eyes, our ears and our minds cannot encompass His greatness. We cannot fathom it. He is greater than what we can even imagine or comprehend. He is perfect in all of His attributes, and no one can praise Him the way He is worthy of — no matter how much someone praises Him, Allah is even greater, deserving of even more praise.

SubhanAllah, walhamdulillah, wa la ilaha illallah, wallahu akbar

When a person says these words, Allah answers. When you say SubhanAllah, Allah says: you have spoken the truth. When you say Alhamdulillah, Allah replies: you have spoken the truth. La ilaha illallah — you have spoken the truth. Allahu Akbar — you have spoken the truth. So busy your tongue with these words.

SubhanAllahi wa bihamdihi, astaghfirullaha wa atubu ilayh

The Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam would say these words a lot, and ‘A’ishah noticed it and asked him about it. He explained that his Lord had informed him that he would see a sign in his ummah, and when he saw it he would often recite these words — as Allah says: when the help of Allah comes and the conquest, and you see people entering the religion of Allah in groups, then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness; indeed He is ever accepting of repentance.

And this shows us a very beautiful lesson. When we see the good result of our efforts — we strive to complete a project and reach its completion, or we complete an act of worship, or we see our child accomplish something we both worked very hard on — what should we do? Glorify Allah and seek forgiveness from Him. Glorify Him: ya Allah, it is only because of You that I was able to do this, so all praise is Yours, all thanks to You, the credit goes to You. And seek forgiveness, because I know my shortcomings and the errors I have made in this journey.

SubhanAllahi wa bihamdihi, ‘adada khalqihi…

Hadith

Once the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam was with Juwayriyah, and in the morning after Fajr she was in her prayer place busy in dhikr. He left, and when he returned after some time she was still sitting there glorifying and praising Allah. He asked her whether she had been sitting there since he left, and she said yes. He then said: since leaving you, I said three times four phrases which, if weighed against all that you have done during this period, would prove to be heavier.

Sometimes you are busy in the morning. If you have young children who are dependent on you, your family needs you in the morning and you do not have the luxury of sitting in your musalla and continuing to worship. So there is a difference between those who know and those who don’t know — when you have knowledge of how to glorify and praise Allah in such beautiful words, you don’t miss out on rewards. So make sure you say these words in the morning no matter how busy you are.

‘Adada khalqihi — I glorify Allah as many times as the number of His creatures. And what is that number? It is immeasurable; we cannot even count, because every second, every moment, more and more creatures are being created. Consider just the number of the angels: thousands worship Allah at Baytul-Ma’mur, and they only get one turn — every day a fresh group comes, and they never return. So multiply the number of days by seventy thousand, and that is just the angels. Then look at the tiniest of creatures, a virus or a bacterium, multiplying so quickly. Allah tells us that none knows the forces of your Lord except He. So you are glorifying Allah limitlessly, infinitely.

Wa rida nafsihi — in accordance with His good pleasure. Meaning I glorify Him with as much glorification and praise as He would be pleased with, what Allah loves for Himself. Basically you are saying that I do not have enough words, and even if I were to sit all day and all night it would not be sufficient — so I praise and glorify Allah as much as He would be pleased with.

Wa zinata ‘arshihi — as much as the weight of His Throne. The Throne is the largest, the biggest creation of Allah. The Kursi is smaller than the Throne, and about the Kursi Allah says that it has the capacity for the heavens and the earth combined — way bigger than the heavens and the earth, more than the known universe. And the ‘Arsh is even greater than that.

Wa midada kalimatihi — equal to the ink that may be used in recording His words. The kalimat of Allah are both kawni and shar’i: the words of His decree, such as Kun, be — which are far too great, far too many, far too powerful to be contained in writing — and the kalimat He has spoken to His chosen slaves, His shari’ah, the books He has revealed, the revelation He has sent. And the words of Allah are so many that we learn in the Qur’an that even if all of the trees were pens and the ocean were ink, and after that the oceans were replenished with seven more oceans, the words of Allah would still not run out.

Allahu akbar kabira, walhamdulillahi kathira…

Allah is truly great; praise be to Allah in abundance; and glory be to Allah in the morning and in the evening. We learn in a hadith that a man said these words at the beginning of salah, and afterwards the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam asked who had said them. The man said he had, and the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam said that the gates of the heavens were opened for these words. Ibn ‘Umar, who was there at the time, said that he never stopped saying these words since he heard that. So say them at the beginning of salah, and especially on the day of ‘Eid, because that is the day of takbirat.

Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika…

Glory and praise is to You, O Allah; blessed is Your name, and exalted is Your majesty; none has the right to be worshipped but You. We can say these words at the beginning of salah.

SubhanAllahi la sharika lah…

Abu Dharr (raḍiyallāhu ‘anhu) reported that these are words Allah loves the most — because in them you are glorifying Allah, you are declaring His oneness, you are saying that He is worthy of all praise, that He is able to do all things, that there is no power and might except with Allah, and again you glorify and praise Allah.

Allahumma lakal-hamdu kulluh, wa ilayka yarji’ul-amru kulluh

O Allah, for You is all praise, and all matters return to You. A man asked the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam to teach him a du’a by which Allah would benefit him — something he could say so that Allah would give him what he was in need of — and the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam taught him these words. Because in them we are not only praising and glorifying Allah, but also expressing His oneness, that to Allah return all matters, and His perfect power — that nothing escapes Allah.

Allahumma Rabbana lakal-hamd…

O Allah, our Lord, for You is praise that would fill the heavens and the earth, and fill that which will please You besides them. We can say these words when we get up from ruku’. Most of the time when people get up from ruku’ they just say Sami’allahu liman hamidah, Rabbana lakal-hamd, which is also good — but we learn that the Prophet salla Allahu 'alayhi wa sallam would also say this: as much praise as would fill the skies, the fill of the earth, and the fill of whatever You wish after that, meaning whatever is greater than the heavens and the earth combined.

SubhanAllahi ‘adada ma khalaq…

Glory be to Allah as much as the number of His creation; glory be to Allah as much as what can fill His creation; glory be to Allah as much as the number of what is in the earth and the sky; glory be to Allah as much as what can fill the sky and the earth; glory be to Allah as much as what can fill His creation; glory be to Allah for all that His Book has enumerated; and glory be to Allah as much as what can fill everything.

May Allah forgive us our sins, and may He give us the ability to glorify Him in the morning and in the evening. May He give us the ability to be of those who remember Him a lot, who call upon Him by His beautiful names. So these words of praise — learn them, memorise them, use them, say them with your heart, and also share them. Teach them to those around you, so that people find closeness to Allah ‘Azza wa Jall.

Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdik, ashhadu an la ilaha illa anta, astaghfiruka wa atubu ilaik.
Wassalamu ‘alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
Chapter Forty-Four

Every Du’a Is Veiled Until Salat Is Sent

Part of our supplication should be that we glorify Allah and praise Him.
